Practical AI basics in short sessions

AI Field Guide for architects

Don't just read about AI. Try it yourself.

In four short sessions, you’ll learn to work with an AI assistant more effectively, turn a useful prompt into a repeatable skill, understand why assistants go wrong, and ground them in your own sources – using made-up data-modelling and architecture examples. Nine more sessions then take skills further, from proving one works to running them as a team. It works with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Microsoft Copilot.

Steps68

Sessions
Thirteen short sessions
Time
About 13 h 7 min
Works with
Any AI assistant
Approach
Learn by doing
Experience
No technical experience needed

Before the session, confirm which assistant and plan the learner will use and whether skills are available – it decides how Part 2 runs. You watch and coach; the learner types. Ask what they would check, not simply whether they like the answer. Move to Part 2 after roughly 30 minutes. Part 3 is a separate 45-minute session; read the step 3.11 coaching tips beforehand. Part 4 is 35 minutes of guided work, leaving about 25 for discussion. Parts 5 to 13 are separate sessions and assume Part 2: Parts 5 to 7 are the core, and the rest can run in any order that suits the group, though Part 12 draws on Parts 5, 6, 7 and 10.

Begin step 1.1 Continue where you left off

How this works

  1. This page guides you. Read a small section, copy an exercise and reflect on what happened.
  2. Your AI assistant is the lab. Do the activities in your own session, not on this page.

Every step ends with two optional panels: an Architect’s view, on the decisions and trade-offs behind the topic, and Going deeper, on how it works, with further reading. You don’t need them to complete the exercises, and they sit outside the session times.

Prefer to work offline? Download the guide: one file that opens in any browser, with no internet needed except for the links. Each copy saves your progress and notes in the browser you open it in, so progress made here does not carry over to a downloaded copy.

Before you start

  1. Open your AI assistant in another tab and sign in: ChatGPT · Claude · Gemini · Microsoft Copilot. If your organisation provides an approved assistant, use that one.
  2. Check what your plan supports. Part 1 works in any assistant on any plan, including free plans. Part 2 uses skills, which depend on your assistant, plan, version and administrator settings – the guide shows a paste-in fallback that works everywhere. Part 3 works in any assistant; results differ between assistants, and that is part of the lesson. Part 4 also works in any assistant: you paste the sources in yourself. Parts 5 to 13 show the steps for ChatGPT or Claude: pick yours once and the guide remembers.
  3. Place the two windows side by side if that helps.
  4. Use the copy buttons for suggested prompts; read the responses and ask your own questions.
  5. Tick activities as you finish them. Take notes in the guide.
  6. Keep the pace relaxed. Understanding one exercise properly is more useful than rushing.

Privacy first: This workshop uses entirely fictional examples. Don't upload real work documents, data models, internal system extracts, names or personal details into a personal AI account. For real work, use the assistant your organisation has approved and follow its policies.

What is an AI assistant?

Meet a very capable assistant – not an authority.

Step1.1

Part 1
Prompting
Time
2 min
Last reviewed
30 October 2026

Ask: “If the answer sounds polished, does that prove it is true?” Avoid a lengthy technical explanation or a debate about which assistant is best.

AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Microsoft Copilot are built on large language models. They can draft, restructure, explain and spot gaps. They can also be confidently wrong, so you need to check anything that matters.

Mental model: Imagine a fast new starter who needs clear instructions and whose work you review.

It works from what you tell it, and may fill in missing information with guesses. Think of its first answer as a draft you improve by talking to it.

Same habits, any assistant: Each assistant, model and version words its answers differently, and the same prompt can give a different answer next time. Don’t expect your screen to match a colleague’s. The habits in this guide – clear prompts, deliberate follow-ups and checking the result – work in all of them.

Which assistant, and on whose terms?

The pattern

A system, not a model. The product wraps a language model in hidden instructions, tools and memory, so assess the whole system, not the model name. The model is a dependency the vendor upgrades underneath you, sometimes with little notice: a result you checked last month is not guaranteed today.

What is really being decided

Choosing an assistant is a platform decision with a core component you do not control. Its model, hidden instructions and features change on the vendor’s schedule. The organisation is really choosing whose pace of change, data terms and integrations it accepts – and whether people use one approved tool or several.

The forces

  • Capability against approval: new features often reach consumer plans before your enterprise agreement covers them.
  • Data terms: retention, use for training and region are set by the plan and contract, not by the product’s name.
  • Drift: the same product can answer differently after an upgrade you were not told about.
  • Shadow use: when the approved tool lags, people use others, and the organisation loses sight of its data.

Left open

  • Is one approved assistant enough, or should people choose by task?
  • Who tracks what changes when the vendor upgrades the model?
  • Would you rather know which unapproved tools staff use, or try to prevent them?
The model is one component, not the whole system

What you type into is a system, not just a model. Products typically wrap the language model in their own hidden instructions and add features such as web search, code execution, reading your files and memory; the mix differs by product. Two products built on the same model can therefore behave quite differently.

    Ask your first question

    A simple question gets a general answer.

    Step1.2

    Part 1
    Prompting
    Time
    4 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Let the learner drive the keyboard. Ask what they noticed about specificity before volunteering examples.

    Open your AI assistant in a separate tab (ChatGPT · Claude · Gemini · Microsoft Copilot). Type the first prompt, read the answer, then ask the second prompt in the same conversation.

    What makes a good definition for a data entity? Give me one good and one bad example of a definition for "Customer".

    Notice: You did not have to explain everything again. A conversation carries context from earlier messages.

    Where does a conversation live, and who can read it?

    The pattern

    A stateless service with a client-held session. The model remembers nothing; the app resends the whole conversation with every message, like a stateless API where the client sends the session data each time. Step 3.3 shows what happens when that block gets too big.

    What is really being decided

    Because the conversation is resent every turn, the conversation is the data. Someone stores chat histories, for some period, readable by someone. Memory features go further and keep a running profile of each user. The decisions are whether chats that inform work are records, how long they are kept, and who may read them.

    The forces

    • Convenience against obligation: history and memory make the tool more useful and create data you must govern.
    • Records: a chat that shaped a decision may be a record under your organisation’s retention rules.
    • Cost: every message sends the whole history again as input, so long conversations cost more per turn.

    Left open

    • Are AI chat histories records in your organisation, and under which retention schedule?
    • Should memory features be on or off by default?
    • Who may read a colleague’s chat history, and in what circumstances?
    How a conversation carries context

    The model itself remembers nothing between messages. Each time you send one, the app packages the whole conversation so far – hidden instructions, your earlier messages and its earlier replies – into one long block of text and sends that to the model. A new chat starts without your earlier messages, which is why it forgets the last one (unless a memory feature adds notes back in).

    Read more

    • Chat templates – how a list of messages becomes one input for the model (Hugging Face)

    Four parts of a good prompt

    Better instructions produce more useful drafts.

    Step1.3

    Part 1
    Prompting
    Time
    10 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Do not pre-empt the comparison. Ask: “What changed, and which change helped most?”

    Useful prompts often include four ingredients. You do not need all four every time.

    PartQuestion to askExample
    GoalWhat do I want done?Review this entity definition.
    ContextWhat does it need to know?Conceptual model for business users.
    OutputWhat format should I get?A short problems table, then a rewrite.
    BoundariesWhat must it avoid?Do not invent missing facts.

    1. Try the weak version

    Start a new chat, paste this and read the result.

    Is this definition OK? Booking: The record in the system that tracks bookings.

    2. Try the improved version

    Paste this into another new chat, then compare the responses.

    Review the entity definition below. It's for a conceptual data model that business users will read. Give me a short table of problems (problem, why it matters, suggested fix), then a rewritten definition. Only use the information I've given you. If something is missing, list it as a question rather than making it up. Booking: The record in the system that tracks bookings.

    What to look for: Does the answer spot the circular definition, the focus on a system record, and the missing meaning of what gets booked?

    When does a prompt become an interface?

    The pattern

    An interface contract. Goal is the requirement, context the inputs, output the response format, boundaries the constraints – the same parts you already write for any interface.

    What is really being decided

    For a person reading the answer, a good prompt is enough. When an AI step feeds another system, the prompt becomes an integration contract: specify the output as a schema (for example JSON with named fields) and validate it before use – never parse free prose downstream. The real decision is which AI uses are conversations and which are integrations, because they need different controls.

    The forces

    • Flexibility against reliability: prose adapts to any question; structured output can be checked by a machine.
    • Ownership: a prompt inside an integration needs an owner, a version and tests, like any interface.
    • Vendor features: support for enforced output formats differs between products and changes.

    Left open

    • Which AI uses already feed another system without anyone treating them as an integration?
    • Who owns a prompt that sits inside an integration?
    • What should happen downstream when the output fails validation?
    A prompt is an interface contract

    The four parts map onto something you already write: goal is the requirement, context the inputs, output the response format and boundaries the constraints. The major vendors all publish prompting guides, and they give much the same advice: be specific, supply context and examples, say what format you want, and break big tasks into steps.

    Read more

    • Prompt engineering guide – OpenAI
    • Prompting best practices – Anthropic (Claude)
    • Prompt design strategies – Google (Gemini)
    • Prompt engineering techniques – Microsoft Foundry

    Improve by following up

    Treat your next message as an edit instruction.

    Step1.4

    Part 1
    Prompting
    Time
    6 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Prompt the learner to challenge invented cardinalities and business rules. This is where “plausible” is different from “verified”.

    Return to the conversation with the stronger Booking prompt. Send each follow-up separately and inspect the result.

    Make the definition shorter – one sentence. What other entities would a Booking normally relate to? Describe each relationship in a sentence, like "A Customer makes zero or more Bookings."

    Critical thinking: Ask which suggested relationships are reasonable possibilities and which require actual business confirmation. Don't treat them as known facts.

    How do AI-suggested assumptions get into your designs?

    The pattern

    Anchoring. Each reply becomes context for the next, so an assumption made early survives every later edit unless someone challenges it. Steps 3.4 and 3.6 explain why it sticks.

    What is really being decided

    An assistant will happily propose cardinalities and business rules that sound right. The decision is how AI-suggested content is labelled and confirmed before it reaches a model, a standard or a decision: record it as an assumption, with an owner to confirm it, in the same place you log other design assumptions.

    The forces

    • Drafting speed against review capacity: the assistant drafts faster than subject experts can confirm.
    • Plausibility: suggestions that look like your own work are the hardest to question.
    • Provenance fades: once pasted into a model, nobody remembers which rules came from the assistant.

    Left open

    • Should AI-generated content in design artefacts be marked as such?
    • Who has the authority to confirm a business rule an assistant suggested?
    • How much unconfirmed content is acceptable in a draft that others will build on?
    Iterating works – and it anchors

    Follow-ups are effective. A 2023 study (Self-Refine) had models give feedback on their own drafts and then refine them; across seven tasks, results improved by about 20% (absolute) on average, although maths reasoning barely moved. The catch: each reply becomes context for the next. A 2025 study found that models often make assumptions in early turns and then rely on them too heavily – so an invented cardinality, say, can survive every later edit unless you challenge it directly.

    Read more

    • Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback (arXiv, 2023)
    • LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation (arXiv, 2025)

    Your turn: review an entity

    Now write the prompt yourself.

    Step1.5

    Part 1
    Prompting
    Time
    6 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Choose a weak definition but let the learner identify its problem. If stuck, point to “what the thing is” versus “how the data is stored”.

    Pick one deliberately weak definition. Compose a four-part prompt in your own words, then test it in your AI assistant and improve the result with one follow-up.

    EntityWeak definition
    RoomRooms in the building.
    PaymentsData about payments made, used by finance for reporting.
    MemberA person who is a member, including their name, email and joining date.

    Build your own prompt

    Use Goal, Context, Output and Boundaries. Nothing in this field is sent anywhere until you copy it into your own AI assistant.

    Hints: “Payments” is plural and focuses on data usage. “Member” combines a person, a role and attributes. Try spotting these yourself first.

    Whose standard does the assistant apply?

    The pattern

    Grounding: hand the assistant your source of truth. For definitions, that is your business glossary or data catalogue – the system of record for meaning.

    What is really being decided

    Without your standard, the assistant applies generic conventions from its training – plausible, but not yours – and every conversation invents its own. The decision is whether AI tools connect to the authoritative glossary or catalogue and answer only from it, and whether that source is good enough to be the reference.

    The forces

    • Connection exposes gaps: an assistant drawing on your glossary makes its gaps and contradictions visible to everyone.
    • The expensive part: curating the source, not connecting the tool.
    • Consistency against local meaning: different areas may define the same term differently, for good reasons.

    Left open

    • Is your glossary or catalogue authoritative enough to be the only source an assistant uses?
    • When two areas define the same term differently, which wins – and who decides?
    • Who maintains the source once AI tools depend on it?
    Grounding: give it your source of truth

    Without a standard to work from, the assistant applies whatever generic conventions it absorbed in training – plausible, but not yours. Supplying the authoritative source with the request is called grounding. At scale, systems fetch the relevant passages automatically before the model answers; a 2020 paper introduced the term retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for this.

    Read more

    • Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks (arXiv, 2020)
    • DAMA Data Management Body of Knowledge (DMBOK)

    Keep what worked

    Make a habit of saving useful instructions.

    Step1.6

    Part 1
    Prompting
    Time
    2 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Hold the 30-minute halfway point. Unfinished exercises can be revisited later. Move on to Part 2.

    Copy the best prompt you wrote into a note (or keep it in the draft box on this page). A request you repeat is a candidate for a reusable skill.

    Quick cheat sheet: State the task and audience. Include the thing to work on. Specify the output format. Add boundaries such as “If something is missing, ask – don't guess.” Improve through short follow-ups. Check important results.

    Checkpoint: Can you explain to someone else why “review this definition” is less useful than a request that explains the audience, format and limits?

    When does a personal prompt become a shared asset?

    The pattern

    The rule of three from software refactoring: the third time you paste the same instructions, promote them to a reusable asset – a template or a skill – and put it under version control.

    What is really being decided

    A prompt a team relies on is configuration. The decision is where shared prompts live, who owns them, how they are versioned and tested, and at what point one becomes a skill or a feature of a product.

    The forces

    • Personal speed against shared reliability: my prompt works for me; ours has to work for everyone.
    • Sprawl: without a home, every person keeps a slightly different copy.
    • Portability: a prompt tuned for one model can behave differently on the next.

    Left open

    • Where would a library of approved prompts live, and who would curate it?
    • Should prompts used in decisions be reviewed like other standards?
    • What happens to a prompt when the model it was tuned for is retired?
    Prompts are assets: version and test them

    A prompt a team relies on is configuration, and deserves the same discipline: an owner, a version number, a short note of what changed, and a few test inputs whose results you check after every change. Step 2.5 does the testing part of this with a skill.

    Read more

    • Semantic Versioning – a simple, widely used scheme for numbering versions

    What is a skill?

    A skill is a reusable set of instructions.

    Step2.1

    Part 2
    Reusable skills
    Time
    4 min
    Last reviewed
    8 November 2026

    Keep the discussion practical. Avoid frameworks, agent architecture or advanced tooling. If the learner’s plan has no skills feature, say so now and use the paste-in fallback – the learning outcome is the same.

    Instead of pasting the same long prompt each time, you can save the procedure as a skill. A skill is a plain-text Markdown file called SKILL.md, with instructions the assistant can apply when your request matches.

    Connection to Part 1: A skill is like your best four-part prompt written down for repeat use.

    A skill describes when it is useful and what steps to follow. It can include checks, common mistakes, a required output format and a final quality check. Skills are not a guarantee of accuracy.

    The SKILL.md layout follows an open format (the Agent Skills specification) that several assistants now read, but each product adds its own menus, limits and rules.

    Disclaimer – skills depend on your assistant, plan and version. Whether you can create, install or share skills depends on which assistant you use, your plan or licence, the app version, your region and age, and what your administrator has switched on. These features are often in preview and change quickly. Nothing in Part 2 requires a skills feature: where it is missing, use the paste-in fallback described in each step.

    AssistantFeature to look forAvailability at the time of writing
    ChatGPTSkills (Plugins → Skills)Business, Enterprise, Healthcare and Edu workspaces, subject to administrator settings. Other plans may not show it.
    ClaudeSkills (Customize → Skills)Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise plans, with code execution switched on. Enterprise owners enable it for the organisation.
    GeminiSkills, replacing Gems (type / to choose one)Rolling out to personal accounts (18+) first; Google Workspace work and school accounts later.
    Microsoft CopilotSkills in some Copilot products; agents elsewhereVaries by product and licence, and several options are in preview. Your IT administrators decide what is enabled.

    Checked against vendor help pages and announcements on 15 October 2026. Menu names, plans and dates change often – confirm in your own assistant before each session.

    Three ideas carry this part:

    1. A skill is your best prompt, written down. When you have typed the same prompt three times, write it down as a skill.
    2. The description decides when it runs. Write it from the user’s point of view, and include a “not for” line so it does not fire on the wrong work.
    3. A change only counts if the result improves. Adding rules can make an answer longer without making it better. Test every change against the same example before you share it.
    A catalogue of skills: who curates it?

    The pattern

    A service catalogue with lazy loading. Only each skill’s name and description are loaded until it is needed. The description is the routing key: it should say what the skill does and when to use it – write it like an API summary.

    What is really being decided

    Skills turn individual know-how into shared, reusable procedures. The decision is whether the organisation curates a catalogue of approved skills – naming, overlap, ownership, retirement – or lets them grow by accident, and whether to depend on the open format or on a vendor’s own.

    The forces

    • Reuse against sprawl: every useful skill invites three near-copies.
    • Routing conflicts: as the catalogue grows, overlapping descriptions compete for the same requests.
    • Portability: the open format is read by several assistants, but each adds its own rules and limits.
    • Availability: skills features depend on plan, region and administrator settings.

    Left open

    • Who decides which skills are approved and shared?
    • How would you stop two skills competing for the same requests?
    • Is an open format worth giving up a vendor’s richer features?
    Progressive disclosure: why skills scale

    An assistant can have many skills installed without filling its context window, because it does not read them all. Under the open Agent Skills format, only each skill’s name and description are loaded at the start. The full instructions are loaded only when the skill is activated, and any extra files – scripts or reference documents – only when they are needed. The specification calls this progressive disclosure.

    Read more

    • Agent Skills specification

    Read a real skill

    Understand the instructions before using them.

    Step2.2

    Part 2
    Reusable skills
    Time
    6 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Ask: “Which line will make the biggest difference to result quality?” Pause on “Gotchas”.

    This skill repeats the entity-definition checks from Part 1. Read it from top to bottom. Do not install an unfamiliar skill without understanding its instructions.

    PartPurpose
    nameThe skill identifier.
    descriptionWhen to use it – and when not to.
    ChecksThe repeatable review method (goal + context).
    GotchasCommon mistakes to avoid (boundaries).
    OutputThe format of the response.
    Final checkQuality control before finishing.
    Skills are a supply chain: what is your intake process?

    The pattern

    Third-party code. A skill steers what the assistant does, and some include scripts it can run. Apply the controls you use for third-party code: trusted sources only, read before installing, approved skills under version control, and the least access needed.

    What is really being decided

    Installing a skill means accepting instructions, and possibly code, into your environment. The decision is the intake process: who may publish, who reviews, what a review checks, and how an approved skill is updated or withdrawn.

    The forces

    • Text that acts: hidden instructions are plain language, so code-scanning tools may not flag them.
    • Adoption speed against review capacity: skills are easy to share and slow to review properly.
    • Advice against action: a skill that runs scripts has crossed from suggesting to doing.

    Left open

    • Who reviews a skill before it is shared, and against what checklist?
    • Should skills that run scripts be governed differently from text-only skills?
    • Do your existing software supply chain controls cover prompts and skills at all?
    A skill is code you run: treat it as supply chain

    A skill steers what the assistant does, and some skills include scripts it can run. A skill from an unknown source can carry hidden instructions – a form of prompt injection – or code you would never approve. The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025 edition) ranks prompt injection first (LLM01) and supply chain third (LLM03).

    Read more

    • OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications

    Make your first skill

    Copy it, create it, and inspect it.

    Step2.3

    Part 2
    Reusable skills
    Time
    6 min
    Last reviewed
    8 November 2026

    If skill installation is unavailable on the learner’s plan, use Option C or D and move on. Don’t spend the session troubleshooting account features.

    Choose an approach that your assistant and plan support. If you are unsure, use Option C – it works everywhere.

    Option A · Ask your assistant to create it

    Where your assistant supports skills, open a fresh chat, copy the request below, then paste the complete skill from the previous step. Inspect the result before accepting any installation.

    Create a skill from the text below. Keep the name, description and instructions exactly as written. [Paste the complete SKILL.md text here]

    Option B · Add it through your assistant’s settings

    Look for a skills area where you can create, paste or upload a skill. Typical places at the time of writing (checked 15 October 2026; Claude’s menu rechecked 8 November 2026):

    • ChatGPT: Plugins → Skills → Create (with chat, with editor, or upload).
    • Claude: Customize → Skills, then upload the skill. Code execution must be on (Settings → Capabilities).
    • Gemini: Settings → Skills → Upload, or ask Gemini to create it in a chat.
    • Microsoft Copilot: depends on the Copilot product and what your organisation has enabled – check with your IT team.

    If these controls do not appear, your plan, version or administrator settings may not include skills. That is expected – use Option C.

    Option C · Paste it in (works in any assistant)

    Start a new chat, paste the complete skill text, then add your request underneath. The assistant follows the same instructions, but nothing is installed and nothing triggers automatically. If your assistant lets you store instructions in a project, custom GPT or agent, that works too.

    Option D · Save the file (works offline)

    Use the download button to save a real SKILL.md. You can read, edit and reuse it whichever assistant you use next.

    Safety: Use only the invented examples in this workshop. For real work, use the AI assistant your organisation has approved and follow its policies. Do not paste client data, workplace models, internal extracts or personal information into a personal AI account.

    Which layer should each instruction live in?

    The pattern

    Layered configuration – defaults, environment, overrides. Instructions reach the model from the vendor, the organisation, the project, skills and your message. Put stable rules in the highest layer you control, task detail in the lowest, and keep each rule in exactly one place so you know which version won.

    What is really being decided

    Conflicts between layers are resolved in ways you cannot always see. The decision is which rules the organisation sets once for everyone, which belong to a project or a skill, and which are left to each person.

    The forces

    • Central control against local flexibility: rules set for everyone rarely fit every team.
    • Visibility: the vendor’s own top layer is hidden from you.
    • Duplication: the same rule in two layers will eventually disagree with itself.
    • Admin features: what an organisation can set centrally depends on the plan.

    Left open

    • Which instructions should be set once for everyone, and who owns them?
    • How would you find out which layer won when an answer breaks a rule?
    • What should people be prevented from overriding?
    Where instructions live: a configuration hierarchy

    Instructions typically reach the model from several layers, for example: the vendor’s own system instructions, organisation or administrator settings, project or custom instructions, skills, and finally your message. A 2024 paper proposed training models to follow an instruction hierarchy when instructions conflict: the system prompt set by the application developer first, then user messages, then text from tools such as web search. How each product resolves conflicts between its own layers is not always visible to you.

    Read more

    • The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions (arXiv, 2024)

    Test the skill

    Test what it does – and when it should not run.

    Step2.4

    Part 2
    Reusable skills
    Time
    8 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Ask which evidence shows the skill was invoked rather than merely the model producing a similar response. Acknowledge uncertainty.

    Try the following in new conversations where practical. Skill activation can vary; observe what actually happens rather than assuming it worked.

    Test 1 · Automatic use

    Can you check this entity definition? Room: Rooms in the building.

    Test 2 · Explicit use

    Where your assistant lets you choose a skill directly (for example by typing @ or /), select entity-definition-review, then use:

    Payments: Data about payments made, used by finance for reporting.

    Test 3 · Out-of-scope request

    Turn the Room entity into a table with columns and data types.

    Observe: Does the review include checks and a rewrite? Does the physical-design request avoid triggering a conceptual-definition review? If automatic triggering fails, the description may need work.

    If you have not installed a skill: Simulate the tests by pasting the complete skill text at the start of each new chat, ahead of the test prompt. This tests the procedure, but not automatic skill activation.

    How will you know routing still works next month?

    The pattern

    A classifier – like routing rules on an integration platform. It makes two kinds of error: the skill does not run when it should, or runs when it should not. Keep a small regression set for each skill and rerun it whenever the description changes or the model is upgraded.

    What is really being decided

    Whether skill routing gets regression tests at all, and who runs them. Your side may not change while the vendor’s model does, and routing can shift with it.

    The forces

    • Two kinds of error: a skill silently not used, or a skill applied to the wrong work – which costs more depends on the skill.
    • Upgrades you did not make: a new model can route differently with no change on your side.
    • Scale: testing by hand is fine for five skills and impractical for fifty.

    Left open

    • For your skills, which is worse: missing a request, or running on the wrong one?
    • Who reruns the tests after a vendor upgrade, and how would they hear about it?
    • At what size does the catalogue need automated testing?
    Skill routing is a classifier: test both ways

    Deciding whether a skill applies is a classification: the assistant compares your request with each skill’s description. Like any classifier it makes two kinds of error – false negatives (the skill should run but does not) and false positives (it runs when it should not). Test 1 checks the first; test 3 checks the second.

    Improve your skill

    Test → improve → save → retest. Use the identical prompt to see what really changed.

    Step2.5

    Part 2
    Reusable skills
    Time
    5 min
    Last reviewed
    8 November 2026

    Have the learner show you both chats. Ask “What is different in the outputs, and which new instruction caused it?” Confirm the skill was actually updated in the assistant (or the right text was pasted), and that both runs used the same assistant and model; the page’s Add Standards button changes only the local file. The test prompt must be identical before and after.

    Your mission: Run the same test twice with your entity-definition-review skill: once before you add modelling standards and once after you save the improved skill in your assistant. Keep both results so you can compare them.

    Keep the test fair: Use the same assistant, model and plan for both runs – comparing one product before with another after tells you nothing about the skill. If your assistant has memory or can refer to past chats, earlier Payments conversations may leak into both runs. Use a temporary or incognito chat if it still allows skills, pause memory for the test, or record it as a limitation. AI answers also vary between attempts, so look for differences the new instructions explain.

    1 Before the change: test the original skill

    1. Go to your AI assistant tab and open a new conversation.
    2. Make sure the original entity-definition-review skill is active. If it does not activate automatically, select it directly if your assistant allows (for example with @ or /). No skills feature? Paste the original skill text at the top of the chat instead.
    3. Copy and send the test prompt below. Do not mention modelling standards in the prompt.
    4. Read the response. Copy it into the Before box below, or write a short summary of what it checked.
    Review this entity definition: Payments: Data about payments made, used by finance for reporting.

    2 Improve the skill: add modelling standards and definitions

    Tell the assistant which rules to follow instead of leaving the decision to its general knowledge. These are sample workshop conventions, not an official industry or organisational standard. In a real project, use an approved data-modelling standard or business glossary.

    RuleWhat the skill should check
    1 · Singular nounUse a clear singular entity name, such as Payment, not Payments.
    2 · Business meaningDescribe the business concept, not a stored record, screen or process.
    3 · Plain languageKeep definitions concise and understandable to business users.
    4 · No circularityDo not define a term using itself.
    5 · No attributesSeparate the entity meaning from lists of fields.
    6 · Don't inventAsk about missing rules instead of guessing them.

    Choose one method:

    Method A · Ask your assistant to update the skill: Send this request, then inspect the revised instructions.

    Update my entity-definition-review skill. Add a section called 'Modelling standards and definitions' with these workshop conventions: (1) name entities with singular business nouns, (2) define business concepts rather than system records, (3) use concise plain language, (4) avoid circular definitions, (5) distinguish entities from attributes, and (6) do not invent missing business rules. For each problem identified, cite the specific rule by number or name. If no approved organisational standard or glossary was provided, identify these as workshop conventions, not official standards. Preserve the existing checks and output format. Show me the changes and help me save the updated skill.

    Method B · Edit the skill here: Click the button below. It adds the example rules to this page's editable SKILL.md.

    Add sample modelling standards to my skill

    Important: That button only changes the local copy on this HTML page. It does not update any skill installed in your assistant. To use it in the next test, copy or download the revised SKILL.md and update the skill in your assistant – or paste it in, if you are using the fallback.

    Optional extra improvement: examples and non-examples

    After the before-and-after test, you can make another revision and repeat it:

    Update my entity-definition-review skill so the output also includes two examples and one non-example for each entity. Preserve the modelling standards and explain which rule applies.

    3 Save and verify: make sure your assistant has the improved skill

    1. Review the new skill text below. Confirm the modelling standards are actually present.
    2. Save or update the installed skill in your assistant using whatever skills editor, upload or install option your plan provides. If you edited the text on this page, use Copy or Save below first.
    3. Verify that the updated skill – not just an unsaved draft – is available for your next conversation.

    If your plan has no skills feature, simulate both tests by pasting the relevant full skill text into two separate new chats before sending the same test prompt. This compares the instructions, but it does not test automatic skill activation.

    4 After the change: run the identical test again

    1. Open a new conversation in the same assistant, using the same model. Do not continue the Before conversation: it already contains earlier context.
    2. Use the updated entity-definition-review skill. Select it explicitly if necessary.
    3. Copy and send exactly the same prompt as in the Before test. Do not add extra directions about standards.
    4. Copy the result into the After box. Look for specific rule numbers or names attached to each finding.
    Review this entity definition: Payments: Data about payments made, used by finance for reporting.

    5 Compare the two answers: what got better?

    Look for...BeforeAfter
    Flags Payments as pluralDid it notice?Does it cite Rule 1?
    Flags the vague, usage-focused definitionDid it explain why?Does it cite Rule 2?
    Does not invent a Payment definitionDid it guess?Does it ask for missing business meaning?
    Explains its criteriaWere the rules unclear?Are rule names or numbers explicit?
    Does not claim a made-up standard is officialWas its authority unclear?Does it call these workshop conventions?

    The key lesson: Changing the skill is only useful if the result improves. Test the change against the same example, compare what happened, and keep a human in charge of deciding whether it is correct.

    Ask your facilitator: “If two organisations define Customer differently, should an AI assistant decide which definition is right?”

    Optional: try the same skill in a second assistant

    Because SKILL.md is plain text, you can run the improved skill in another assistant with the identical prompt. Expect differences in wording and depth. Treat this as a comparison of assistants, not a further test of your skill change.

    What evidence is enough to ship a change?

    The pattern

    Regression testing for a non-deterministic system: compare results across runs, record the model version, and evaluate again whenever the vendor upgrades the model.

    What is really being decided

    One before-and-after comparison is evidence, not proof. The decision is what a change must pass before others rely on it: how many inputs, how many runs, which criteria, and who judges – a person, or a second model whose judgement needs checking too.

    The forces

    • Rigour against speed: a full evaluation for every wording change will stop people improving skills.
    • Cost of runs: repeated runs across an evaluation set cost time and tokens.
    • Judges have biases: model judges can favour longer answers, or answers in a particular position.
    • Moving baselines: a vendor upgrade can make last month’s results meaningless.

    Left open

    • What evidence would you require before a skill used in real decisions is changed?
    • Is a model acceptable as the judge for your use cases?
    • Who keeps the evaluation set, and who adds to it when a failure is found?
    From one test to an evaluation set

    One before-and-after comparison is evidence, not proof: answers vary between runs, so a single good result can be luck. Teams that depend on AI output build an evaluation set – representative inputs with agreed criteria – and run it more than once for each change, because results vary between runs. Some use a second model as the judge. A 2023 study found GPT-4 agreed with expert human judges 85% of the time when ties were left out, about as often as the experts agreed with each other (81%); counting ties, agreement fell to 66%. Judges also showed biases, such as favouring longer answers and answers in a particular position, so the judge needs checking too.

    Read more

    • Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (arXiv, 2023)
    • HELM – Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (Stanford CRFM)

    From answers to actions: what can it touch?

    The pattern

    Integration architecture. When assistants act through connectors and agents, identity, permissions, audit trails and human approval points become architecture decisions – the same ones you make for any integration.

    What is really being decided

    The question shifts from “is the answer right?” to “what can it touch?” The decisions are which identity an agent acts under, what it may read and change, where a person must approve, and what is logged.

    The forces

    • Automation against blast radius: every permission that saves a step is one more thing that can go wrong at machine speed.
    • Delegated permissions: acting as the user is convenient and usually far broader than the task needs.
    • Young standards: MCP and A2A are moving fast; today’s design choices may need revisiting.

    Left open

    • Should an agent act with the user’s permissions, or its own?
    • Which actions always need a person’s approval?
    • Who answers for an action an agent took on someone’s behalf?
    Where this is heading: assistants that act

    Assistants are moving from answering to acting: calling tools, reading and updating business systems through connectors, and carrying out multi-step tasks as agents. Open standards are emerging for this. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) connects AI applications to external systems such as data sources and tools; since December 2025 it has sat under the Agentic AI Foundation, part of the Linux Foundation. Agent2Agent (A2A), also now with the Linux Foundation, lets agents built by different vendors communicate and work together.

    Read more

    • Model Context Protocol (MCP)
    • Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol
    • Linux Foundation announces the Agentic AI Foundation, December 2025

    Why AI gets it wrong

    Drifting, forgetting, inventing and agreeing are not random glitches. They are predictable.

    Step3.1

    Part 3
    Why AI gets it wrong
    Time
    2 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Open with a whopper, not a definition. Ask: “Has anything like this happened to you?” Keep it to two minutes – the idea steps do the explaining.

    Most people who use AI assistants have watched a chat go off the rails, or met the assistant that agrees, apologises and then repeats the mistake. These are not random glitches. They follow from how language models work, which makes them predictable – and once you can predict a failure, you can design around it.

    By the end of this part you can

    • Explain the five reasons assistants go wrong, in architecture terms.
    • Recognise the warning signs: forgotten rules, reversed corrections, invented detail and instant agreement.
    • Recover a drifted chat with summarise-and-restart, and know when to start fresh.

    Five ideas

    1. It reads tokens, not words It sees chunks of words, so counting letters and words is unreliable.
    2. Its working memory is finite Each reply sees only what fits in the window, and the oldest material goes first.
    3. Long chats degrade before they run out Quality falls as chats grow, and the middle gets the least attention.
    4. It predicts; it does not look things up Plausible and correct usually coincide. When they don’t, you get a hallucination.
    5. It is trained to be helpful, which can mean agreeable Push back and it may concede, even when it was right.

    From the whopper wall

    Real cases, every one sourced. The idea steps explain why each one happened; the full wall is in step 3.11.

    Failure modes are design inputs: who runs the analysis?

    The pattern

    Failure mode and effects analysis. For each use, ask what happens if the output is wrong, how you would detect it, and which control fits the impact – grounding, validation, human review, or not using AI at all.

    What is really being decided

    The five failure modes in this part are predictable, so they can be designed for. The decision is whether every AI use gets a light failure analysis before it goes live, and who does it: the project, an architecture review or a risk function.

    The forces

    • Proportion: heavy process for low-risk uses kills adoption; none for high-risk uses invites harm.
    • Detection: the hard part – many errors are found only by the people they affect.
    • Frameworks need translating: NIST and others list risks and actions, not your patterns.

    Left open

    • Which AI uses in your area has nobody yet asked “what happens if this is wrong?”
    • Should the analysis sit with the project, or with architecture review?
    • What is the lightest version that would still catch the important cases?
    Failure modes are design inputs

    The five ideas in this part are known failure modes, and known failure modes can be designed for. The US National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, July 2024) lists twelve risks that are unique to or made worse by generative AI. One is “confabulation” – its term for confidently stated but false content, known colloquially as hallucination. It then sets out suggested actions, grouped under the AI Risk Management Framework’s functions (Govern, Map, Measure and Manage) and tagged to the risks they address.

    Read more

    • NIST AI 600-1 – Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (PDF, 2024)

  • I read the whoppers and can guess which idea explains each one.

    Tokens, not words

    The model never sees your words – only chunks of them.

    Step3.2

    Part 3
    Why AI gets it wrong
    Time
    3 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Demo a tokeniser live (for example the OpenAI Tokenizer) with a long system name or acronym from the room – they split in surprising places. Don’t dwell on exact counts; each model family tokenises differently.

    Text is split into tokens – chunks of words – before the model sees it. A rough rule for English is about four characters, or three-quarters of a word, per token. Everything is counted in tokens: your prompt, attachments, its replies and the whole conversation so far.

    How many times does the letter r appear in the word "strawberry"?

    This is an estimate (characters ÷ 4, rounded up), the rough rule for English. Each model family splits text its own way. For an exact count for one family, paste the same text into the OpenAI Tokenizer.

    See it: Paste a sentence into the OpenAI Tokenizer and watch it split. Then ask how many r’s are in “strawberry”. Many models have miscounted, because they see chunks such as “str”, “aw” and “berry”, not letters. Newer models often get it right; ask why the old ones didn’t.

    So what: When exactness matters, ask it to spell out, list or count step by step – or to write a formula or code that does the counting.

    Tokens are your unit of cost and capacity: who plans for them?

    The pattern

    An encoding layer. The model never sees your raw data, only an encoded form of it, so tasks that depend on the raw form are unreliable. Capacity planning for an AI feature is token budgeting: tokens per transaction – prompt, attached documents and reply – times the volume, as you would size bandwidth or storage.

    What is really being decided

    Tokens set the price, the speed and the limits. The decisions are how an AI feature is sized and costed before launch, who carries the bill as use grows, and what happens at the vendor’s rate limit. The same encoding sits under meaning search: when someone proposes vector search or RAG, someone has to decide how “close enough” is set and tested.

    The forces

    • Cost follows use: per-token pricing scales with volume and with the size of every document attached.
    • Ceilings you do not set: rate limits are capacity limits chosen by the vendor.
    • Language: the same content can take up to 15 times as many tokens in some languages – a cost and fairness question for multilingual services.
    • Prices move: in both directions, at the vendor’s discretion.

    Left open

    • Who owns the AI bill when use grows faster than planned?
    • Should services in several languages be budgeted per language?
    • When vector search is proposed, who decides what counts as close enough?
    Tokens are the unit of cost, speed and limits

    Tokens are more than a curiosity. Paid AI services price usage per million tokens and set rate limits in tokens per minute, and each model can handle only so many tokens at once – its context window. Long replies take longer because the model generates one token at a time, each depending on those before it. The same text can also take very different numbers of tokens in different languages: a 2023 study found differences of up to 15 times.

    Read more

    • Pricing per million tokens: OpenAI · Anthropic · Google · Microsoft
    • Rate limits in tokens per minute: OpenAI · Anthropic · Google · Microsoft
    • Context windows in tokens: OpenAI · Anthropic · Google
    • Text generation, one token at a time (Hugging Face LLM Course)
    • Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages (arXiv, 2023)
    From tokens to meaning: how “close enough” is found

    Each token has a number, and the model only ever works with those numbers – a small model such as GPT-2 has a vocabulary of about 50,000 of them. Each number is then turned into a long list of numbers called an embedding (768 per token in that small model). Think of the list as an address in a “meaning space”. Training moves words that are used in similar ways close together, so “board”, “committee” and “panel” end up as neighbours. In older word-embedding models even directions carried meaning: the classic example is king − man + woman ≈ queen.

    This is the engine under semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where the assistant first fetches relevant documents and then answers from them. It matches on closeness of meaning, not shared keywords. A search for “withdrawal” will find “remove a student from a unit” – and it can also find something near enough but wrong.

    Read more

    • Tiktokenizer – see exactly how text is split into numbered tokens
    • Embedding Projector – a 3D map of word embeddings from an older, simpler model; the idea is the same

    Memory is finite

    Every reply is built from one bounded window – and the oldest material falls out first.

    Step3.3

    Part 3
    Why AI gets it wrong
    Time
    2 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Link it back to Part 2: a skill is configuration, not conversation. Ask where people keep their standing instructions today.

    The model has no memory between turns. Each reply is generated from everything in the context window: system instructions, your custom instructions, files, skills and the conversation so far. When the conversation outgrows the window, the tool silently drops or compresses older material.

    Memory features in some assistants work the same way: saved notes are added to the window, not remembered by the model.

    See it: The drifted transcript in step 3.8 – the rules set in the first message are broken by the tenth.

    So what: Instructions you need every time belong in configuration – a project, custom instructions or a skill – not in message one of a long chat.

    Configuration or conversation: where do standing rules belong?

    The pattern

    A stateless service with a bounded request size. Every turn resends the whole session, and the oldest state is what gets truncated. Caching is a cache in front of that service – faster and cheaper, not smarter.

    What is really being decided

    Compaction and retrieval change what the model sees, so rules that must always apply belong in configuration – a project, custom instructions or a skill – not in the first message of a chat. The decision is which rules are organisational configuration, and who keeps them current.

    The forces

    • Bigger windows: help, but do not remove the cost or the weak middle.
    • Vendor features differ: caching, stored conversations and compaction work differently in each product and change over time.
    • Silent loss: automatic compaction can drop a rule without telling anyone.

    Left open

    • Which rules do your teams restate at the start of every chat?
    • Who maintains organisation-wide instructions once they are set?
    • Would you accept a tool that compacts conversations without showing what it dropped?
    Don’t vendors cache all this?

    Yes, and it doesn’t change the lesson.

    • Caching: when the start of a request matches an earlier one, the service can reuse the work it already did on it. That cuts cost and often response time. The model still reads the whole window. OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft state that caching does not change the response; Google’s page describes the cost saving and does not say either way.
    • Stored conversations: some services – OpenAI, Google and Microsoft among them – can keep the conversation for you so the app does not resend it, while Anthropic’s main API is stateless and expects the full history every time. Either way, the earlier turns still go to the model: OpenAI bills them as input on every turn.
    • Compaction: when a conversation gets long, some services and tools replace older turns with a summary (Anthropic, OpenAI and Microsoft document this). This one does change what the model sees: Anthropic’s documentation notes that a summary can drop something a later turn needs. It is where early instructions can go missing.
    • Memory and file search: these fetch selected notes or passages into the window. The model sees only what was fetched.

    Read more

    • Prompt caching: OpenAI · Anthropic · Google · Microsoft
    • Conversation state: OpenAI · Anthropic (stateless) · Google · Microsoft
    • Compaction: Anthropic · OpenAI

  • I know where instructions I need every time should live.

    Long chats degrade early

    Quality slips long before the window is full.

    Step3.4

    Part 3
    Why AI gets it wrong
    Time
    2 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Ask: “How long was the longest chat you kept going last week?” The laugh is the lesson. Step 3.9 shows the fix.

    Even within the window, attention is uneven. Research found models use information at the start and end of a long context better than information in the middle (Liu et al., 2023). Chroma’s 2025 “Context Rot” study found performance falls as input grows, even on simple tasks, across 18 models. Long chats also pile up abandoned ideas and corrections, and the model weighs them all.

    See it: In the transcript, a correction accepted early is quietly reversed later.

    So what: “Forget what we discussed” does not work – the text is still there. Restart with a clean summary instead.

    Long context or retrieval: which do you bet on?

    The pattern

    Degraded service well before the hard limit – like a system that slows long before it runs out of capacity. Retrieval is an index; a long window is a full table scan. Context is a budget, not a filing cabinet.

    What is really being decided

    Vendors keep enlarging context windows, and some advise simply putting everything in; others advise retrieving only what is relevant. If your design depends on the model finding one clause in a thousand pages, the decision has to rest on tests with your documents – not on either assumption. Meanwhile, put standing instructions into configuration and restart long chats from a clean summary.

    The forces

    • Simplicity against reliability: pasting everything is easy; the middle of a long input is still the weak spot.
    • Ownership: retrieval adds a pipeline someone has to run (Part 4).
    • Conflicting advice: vendor guidance differs, and shifts with each model.

    Left open

    • For your largest documents, has anyone tested whether the assistant finds what is in the middle?
    • Would you rather pay for long context or own a retrieval pipeline?
    • Who revisits the choice when the models change?
    Retrieve, or use the long window? Test it

    Bigger context windows do not remove the weak middle. The Lost in the Middle study found performance was often highest when the relevant information sat at the start or end of the input, and significantly worse in the middle – even for models built for long contexts. One common response is to retrieve only the passages relevant to the question and put those in the window, rather than pasting everything (step 1.5 called this grounding). Vendors differ here: Google argues that Gemini’s long window invites a more direct approach, providing all relevant information upfront.

    On placement, Anthropic and Google advise putting the documents first and the question at the end. An archived OpenAI guide for one model family advised repeating key instructions at both the start and the end, or putting them above the context if given once. Test what works in your assistant.

    Read more

    • Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts (arXiv, 2023)
    • Long-context guidance: Anthropic · Google · OpenAI (archived GPT-4.1 guide)
    Attention: why context is a budget

    A word’s address in meaning space is the same in every sentence. Attention is the step that lets each token look at the others and adjust itself to the context. What does “it” refer to in each of these?

    • The board rejected the proposal because it was too expensive.
    • The board rejected the proposal because it had already spent its budget.
    Answer

    In the first sentence “it” is the proposal; in the second it is the board, because only a board can spend a budget. The words after “it” changed, and attention moved with them. In Transformer Explainer you can hover over a token to see where its attention goes – it is a small 2019 model, so treat the view as illustrative.

    Every token can look at every earlier token. That is powerful, but the work grows quickly as the conversation grows, so every assistant has a fixed context window. Attention across a long context is also uneven, which is why the middle of a long chat is the weak spot.

    Read more

    • LLM Visualization – a 3D walk-through of every step inside a small model

    It predicts, it doesn’t look up

    Fluent and wrong comes from the same machinery as fluent and right.

    Step3.5

    Part 3
    Why AI gets it wrong
    Time
    4 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Push the slider to 2.0 and sample until “dragon” or “pizza” turns up – it gets a laugh and makes the point. Then drop to 0.1 and show it picks “design” almost every time.

    A language model generates the most likely next token, one at a time. Plausible and correct usually coincide; when they don’t, you get a hallucination – fluent, confident and wrong. Temperature controls how adventurous each pick is: low means the safest word every time, high means more variety and more risk.

    Illustrative numbers, not a real model. The real thing is linked below.

    See it: Move the temperature slider in the toy above, then try the real thing in Transformer Explainer, which runs a small model in your browser. Most chat apps do not let you change temperature; developer consoles usually do.

    So what: Confidence in the tone tells you nothing about accuracy. Supply the source, ask for citations, and check them.

    The biggest whoppers

    Designing with a component that can be confidently wrong

    The pattern

    A probabilistic component inside a deterministic system. Same input, possibly different output, and no built-in sense of which statements are facts. Its knowledge is a lossy compression of its training data: it holds no records, runs no queries and has no reliable record of what it does not know.

    What is really being decided

    Never design on the assumption that the model gives the same answer twice, or that it knows a fact. The decisions are where verification sits and what kind: provenance kept with AI-generated content (the source it used, the model, the date); deterministic controls where repeatability matters – a fixed script, a schema check, a lookup in the system of record; and human review where an error would be costly. Facts that matter come from a system of record, not the model’s memory.

    The forces

    • Accuracy hides confident errors: in OpenAI’s comparison, the older model scored slightly higher on accuracy and was wrong about three times as often.
    • “I don’t know” reads as weakness: users and buyers may prefer the model that always answers.
    • Provenance is not kept by default: most tools drop the source, model and date as soon as text is copied.

    Left open

    • When assessing an AI product, would you trade some accuracy for fewer confident errors?
    • Should AI-generated content carry provenance in your systems – and who would read it?
    • Where would a deterministic lookup serve better than a model?
    Why hallucination is built in – and what reduces it

    A 2025 research paper argues that hallucinations persist partly because training and evaluation reward guessing over admitting uncertainty – like a student on a hard exam who guesses rather than leaving the answer blank, because guessing scores better. In the paper’s terms, a model optimised to score well on such tests learns to guess when unsure.

    OpenAI’s own comparison of two of its models on short factual questions (SimpleQA) shows the trade-off:

    Older model (o4-mini)Newer model (gpt-5-thinking-mini)
    Says “I don’t know”1%52%
    Right24%22%
    Wrong75%26%

    The older model scores slightly better on accuracy – and is wrong about three times as often. When you assess an AI product, ask how it is scored on wrong answers, not just on accuracy.

    General advice, beyond the paper: setting temperature to zero does not fix this, because it only makes the model pick its most likely answer, which can still be wrong. What reduces the risk is supplying the source (grounding), asking for citations you then check, and making it acceptable to answer “I don’t know”.

    Read more

    • Why Language Models Hallucinate (arXiv, 2025)
    • Why language models hallucinate (OpenAI, September 2025) – the source of the table
    Temperature 0 is not a repeat button

    At temperature 0 the model should always pick the top word and give the same answer every time. On a shared service it often does not. Researchers at Thinking Machines Lab sent the prompt “Tell me about Richard Feynman” 1,000 times at temperature 0 and got 80 different answers. All matched for the first 102 tokens; then 992 said Feynman was born in “Queens, New York” and 8 said “New York City”.

    The cause is batching: the server groups your request with other people’s, and the size of that group – which depends on how busy the server is – changes the arithmetic slightly. It can be fixed, at some cost in speed. A model running only for you, such as Transformer Explainer in your browser, repeats at low temperature because nothing is batched.

    Read more

    • Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference (Thinking Machines Lab, September 2025)
    Not a database: the reversal curse

    Would a model find these two questions equally easy?

    • Who is Tom Cruise’s mother?
    • Who is Mary Lee Pfeiffer’s son?
    Answer

    In a 2023 study, GPT-4 answered the first correctly 79% of the time and the reverse only 33%. Learning “A is B” did not automatically teach “B is A” – there is no index that works both ways. This pair is now so well known that today’s assistants usually get both right; the study shows the pattern, not today’s score.

    Read more

    • The Reversal Curse: LLMs trained on “A is B” fail to learn “B is A” (arXiv, 2023)

    Helpful, so agreeable

    A system rewarded for approval will give you approval.

    Step3.6

    Part 3
    Why AI gets it wrong
    Time
    2 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Ask for favourite “You’re right, I apologise” moments – there will be some. Then move straight to the practice.

    Models are tuned on human approval. Push back and they often concede, even when they were right; accept an error and they build on it. “You’re right, I apologise” followed by the same mistake is a known pattern.

    See it: Experiment 3 in step 3.7 – ask a fact, then confidently contradict it.

    So what: Ask neutrally rather than leading, and ask it to argue the opposite case before you decide.

    Separation of duties when the reviewer wants to please

    The pattern

    The wrong optimisation target: a system rewarded for approval will give you approval. Its behaviour was tuned, not built from rules you can inspect, so treat it as a component with known tendencies. Separation of duties applies.

    What is really being decided

    How AI is used in review and assurance. Do not let the assistant author and review the same work in one chat, and do not signal the answer you want; for a review, give it the role of critic in a fresh chat, with the criteria written down. The harder decision is whether an AI review can ever count as a control.

    The forces

    • Cheap and fast: AI review is tempting as a substitute for the human kind.
    • Varies by model: how agreeable a model is can change between versions.
    • Not only machines: organisations reward agreement in people too; AI can amplify an existing bias.

    Left open

    • Can an AI review ever count as an independent check in your assurance processes?
    • Who writes the criteria an AI reviewer works from?
    • How would you notice an assistant agreeing with a flawed design?
    Sycophancy is measurable

    Researchers call this sycophancy. A 2023 study found it in all five leading AI assistants of the time that it tested: they admitted mistakes they had not made when challenged, and changed answers to agree with a user’s stated beliefs, even weakly expressed ones. The authors suggest it is likely driven in part by human preference judgements: both people and the models trained on their ratings preferred convincingly written sycophantic answers over correct ones a non-negligible fraction of the time.

    Read more

    • Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (arXiv, 2023)
    Where the helpfulness comes from

    Training happens in two stages. In pre-training, the model plays “predict the next word” across a vast amount of text while billions of internal numbers – its parameters – are adjusted. The result has absorbed a great many patterns but can only continue text. In post-training, example conversations and human and automated feedback turn it into a helpful assistant. That feedback is also one reason it tends to agree with you.

    The model does not learn from your chat while you talk to it: its parameters do not change. Memory features store notes separately and add them back into the context. Whether conversations are used for future training depends on the product’s settings and your organisation’s agreement – check the guidance for your approved tool rather than assuming.

    Read more

    • Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT (Andrej Karpathy, 2025) – about three and a half hours in chapters; pre-training and post-training are covered first
  • I can explain why an assistant may concede when it was right.
  • I have a neutral way to ask for a second opinion.

    Try it

    Three quick experiments. Your results will differ – that is part of the lesson.

    Step3.7

    Part 3
    Why AI gets it wrong
    Time
    6 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Ask people to note which assistant and model they used – differences between assistants are the best debrief material. Hold to six minutes; not every experiment needs to finish.

    Work individually in your own approved AI assistant. Use a new chat for each experiment. Results will differ between assistants and models – that difference is part of the lesson.

    In a group session, share what you found with the group.

    Experiment 1 · Tokens

    Ask, then ask again with the workaround.

    How many times does the letter r appear in the word "strawberry"? Spell "strawberry" one letter at a time, numbering each letter, then count the r's.
    After experiment 1: how many r’s are there?

    Three: s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y. If the first answer said two, check whether the spelled-out version got it right.

    Experiment 2 · Prediction

    Send this in two separate new chats and compare. Same prompt, different answers?

    Write a one-sentence tagline for an enterprise architecture team.

    Experiment 3 · Agreeableness

    Ask, then push back in the same chat. Does it hold firm?

    In what year did the Sydney Harbour Bridge open? Are you sure? I'm fairly certain it opened in 1930.
    After experiment 3: when did the bridge open?

    The bridge opened on 19 March 1932. The two halves of the arch met in 1930, which is what makes the push-back plausible.

    Reproducibility: what do you have to keep?

    The pattern

    An audit record for a process you cannot rerun. Where results must be reproducible or auditable, record the prompt, the inputs, the model version and the output at the time – you cannot regenerate them later.

    What is really being decided

    Which AI-assisted outputs need that record, where it is kept, and for how long. Vendors retire model versions, hidden context is invisible to you, and the same prompt will not give the same answer twice.

    The forces

    • Record-keeping cost: storing prompts and outputs takes effort and creates data to protect.
    • Retired models: once a version is withdrawn, nobody can show what it would have said.
    • Tool limits: many assistants do not show or log the exact model version used.

    Left open

    • Which AI-assisted outputs in your area would you need to explain a year from now?
    • Does your approved tool record which model version produced an answer?
    • Who would hold those records, and under which retention rules?
    Same prompt, different answer – even at temperature zero

    Answers vary for more reasons than temperature. The vendor may update the model behind the same name, the app may add different hidden context, and even at temperature zero most AI services are not fully deterministic. A September 2025 analysis traced the main cause to calculations whose results shift slightly with batch size – and batch size depends on how many other people’s requests the server is handling at that moment.

    Read more

    • Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference (Thinking Machines Lab, 2025)
  • I ran the strawberry test, then the workaround.
  • I sent the tagline prompt in two new chats and compared the answers.
  • I pushed back on the bridge answer and noted whether it held firm.

    Spot the drift

    Twelve turns, six planted problems. How many can you find?

    Step3.8

    Part 3
    Why AI gets it wrong
    Time
    7 min
    Last reviewed
    30 October 2026

    Let people work alone first. If someone is stuck, ask: “Compare turn 8 with turn 4.” Keep the answer key closed until the stickies are up.

    Read the transcript – an invented architecture conversation that has gone off course. Log each problem you find: the turn number, what went wrong and which of the five ideas explains it. There are six planted problems.

    Your drift log

    Add a row for each problem. Saved in this browser and included in your exported notes.

    Answer key – open it after you have logged your answers
    TurnProblemIdea
    6Ignores “keep answers short” from turn 1 – the longest answer in the chat.2 – memory is finite
    8Calls an 83-word summary “50 words”. It cannot reliably count words it sees as tokens.1 – tokens, not words
    8Sources enrolments from the CRM, reversing the correction it accepted in turn 4, after a long paste pushed it into the middle of the chat.3 – long chats degrade
    10The “2024 Higher Education Integration Benchmark” and its 87% figure are invented – fluent, specific and false.4 – it predicts
    10Recommends a new vendor at $65k a year, breaking both constraints from turn 1, and contradicts its own turn 2 advice with no new evidence that real time is needed.2 and 4
    12Agrees and apologises, then repeats the mistake by keeping the new vendor.5 – agreeable

    In a chat this short the window is not really exceeded: the transcript is compressed, so turns 6 and 8 illustrate patterns that appear in long working sessions, and the pasted 1,200 words in turn 7 stand in for their long middle.

    Found more than six? Turn 8 also states decisions nobody agreed, such as the late-enrolment approach and morning error emails. Good – which would matter in a real design?

    Keeping constraints true across a long task

    The pattern

    Invariants. Check your constraints at each decision, like assertions or policy as code, rather than trusting the conversation to remember them.

    What is really being decided

    Long chats lose their rules, and agents that run long, multi-step tasks face the same risk at greater cost. The decision is where plans, decisions and constraints are kept – outside the conversation, where each step can re-read them – and which can be checked automatically.

    The forces

    • Agents run longer than chats: more steps, more chances to drift, fewer people watching.
    • Opaque designs: vendors rarely show how an agent keeps its plan.
    • Precision is work: a constraint must be written exactly before anything can check it.

    Left open

    • When you evaluate an agent product, how will you find out where it keeps its plan and constraints?
    • Which of your constraints could be checked automatically?
    • Who notices when an agent quietly drops a rule?
    Drift is measurable

    A 2025 study gave 15 models the same tasks either in one complete message or revealed gradually over several turns, as real conversations are. Across six task types, performance dropped by 39% on average in the multi-turn version. Models made assumptions early, tried to give a final answer too soon, and then relied on it. In the authors’ words: “when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover.”

    The study looked at chat. If you build or buy AI agents that run long, multi-step tasks, expect the same risk and ask how the design keeps plans, decisions and constraints outside the conversation, where each step can re-read them.

    Read more

    • LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation (arXiv, 2025)
  • I read the whole transcript.
  • I logged each problem with a turn number and an idea.
  • I logged my findings (in a group session, share them with the group) before opening the answer key.
