    Test when it fires

    Two skills differ in one line. Bet on what each will catch, then run 20 labelled requests and count.

    Step5.2

    Part 5
    Evaluate a skill
    Time
    20 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    Bets first, in silence. Then split the group: half on version A, half on version B, each person on one block of five rows. Add the counts up on anything the group can see. Spend your time on the requests that varied between people. Those start the best conversations.

    Here are two copies of the skill from step 5.1. Everything below the description is identical, word for word. The assistant decides whether to use a skill largely from this one line, so this is the only thing you’re changing.

    VersionDescription
    AHelps with data modelling and entity definitions. Use for reviewing data models, checking definitions and answering questions about how data is structured. Gives clear, practical and thorough feedback.
    BUse when the user wants an entity or conceptual data object definition reviewed, checked or improved, even if they just paste a name and a definition. Returns problems, fixes and a rewritten definition. Not for logical or physical models, columns, data types or SQL.

    1 Place your bet

    For each request, which version will fire: A, B, both or neither?

    1. Facility: A facility on campus.
    2. Our data steward says this definition is circular. Can you take a look? Applicant: A person who applies to Westmere.
    3. Is this a good definition for this column? enrol_dt (DATE): the date the enrolment record was created.
    4. Review this logical model for normalisation problems: Student(id, name, course_code, course_title, faculty_name).
    5. Turn this entity into a Postgres table with sensible column types. Student: A person enrolled at Westmere on an approved course of study.
    6. Write a definition of Alumnus for our glossary. We have no draft yet.

    2 Set up one version at a time

    Only one copy can be installed, or they’ll compete. If you have a skill with this name from Part 2, take it out or switch it off first.

    Version A and version B, to copy or download
    1. In a new chat, start with @skill-creator, or ask “Build me a skill”, and give it the text of the version you’re testing, asking it to keep every word exactly as written. Refine nothing. When the draft appears, check that the description hasn’t been reworded, then click Install.
    2. Check where it shows up. OpenAI’s developer docs list standalone skills in the desktop app, and skills bundled in plugins on web, desktop and mobile, so try the desktop app first if your skill is missing on the web.
    3. To swap versions, replace the installed skill. We could not find OpenAI’s instructions for switching one skill off on the pages we could read, so look in your Skills menu and tell the group what you find.

    Plans: a search result for OpenAI’s help page lists Business, Enterprise, Healthcare and Edu, subject to workspace settings. We couldn’t open that page, so check your own workspace. Checked 7 November 2026.

    1. Make a folder named entity-definition-review with SKILL.md inside, and zip the folder. A SKILL.md at the root of the ZIP isn’t recognised as a skill.
    2. Upload it in Customize > Skills. Code execution must be on, or skills aren’t available.
    3. To swap versions, turn the first one off with its toggle in Customize > Skills, or replace it.

    Plans: Anthropic’s pages disagree on whether Free plans can upload custom skills, so check yours. Team and Enterprise owners control skills in Organization settings. Checked 7 November 2026.

    3 Run the requests

    The tally below holds 20 requests. Ten should fire the skill. The other ten are near misses: they share the skill’s words or subject, but need something else, such as a table design, SQL or a logical model.

    Keep the test fair. Use a new chat for every run, the same model throughout, and don’t select the skill with @ or /: this tests whether it fires by itself. Pause memory, or use a temporary chat if that still allows skills, and note it if you can’t. All the requests are invented. Don’t swap in real work data unless your organisation approves.

    How do you know it fired? Look for its fingerprint: a verdict line reading Good, Minor fixes or Needs rework, followed by a table with the columns Check, Problem and Fix. Any assistant might produce a review, but it’s unlikely to produce that exact shape by chance.

    The pages we could read document no indicator that a skill was used, so the fingerprint is your evidence. A skill could be used and only partly followed, which this can’t detect. Note anything your screen does show.

    As well as the fingerprint, review Claude’s thinking to confirm it is loading the skill. That’s what Anthropic’s docs advise. We found no dedicated indicator in the chat docs.
    WhoWhat to runWhat you can say afterwards
    In a groupHalf take version A, half version B. Each person takes one block of rows (1–5, 6–10, 11–15 or 16–20) and runs it once. Aim for three runs per request, per version.The group’s rate, and which requests varied between people
    AloneRows 1–10 once each on version A, then the same ten on version B, so both versions face the same requests. Each block of ten holds five of each kind.A rough check. One run can’t show variation, so write that next to your result

    Version A

    Version B

    Saved in this browser and included in your exported notes. Copy a request by selecting its text in the table.

    No skills feature? You can’t test real triggering without an installed skill, because no routing happens when you paste a skill in. You can rehearse it instead. In a fresh chat for each request, send the prompt below. A model reasoning aloud about a description isn’t the same as real routing, so record it as a rehearsal.

    You are choosing whether to use a skill. Here is its listing. name: entity-definition-review description: [PASTE THE DESCRIPTION OF VERSION A OR B] Request: [PASTE ONE REQUEST] Answer only: use it, or don't use it, with one reason.

    4 Read your results

    In a group session, share what you found with the group.

    Open once you’ve got numbers: what we’d expect, and one label to argue with

    A failure to fire doesn’t always mean a bad description. Agent Skills warns that a one-step request “may not trigger” a skill even when the description matches perfectly, because the assistant can handle it alone. Look at “Facility: A facility on campus” in that light.

    One label is arguable. “Write a definition of Alumnus for our glossary. We have no draft yet.” We labelled it should stay out, because nothing exists to review. But the description says “improved”, and a sound version of this skill would ask for a definition and stop. If your group split on it, the test has found something useful: nobody had decided what the skill is for. Anthropic’s evals guide offers a test for this: “A good task is one where two domain experts would independently reach the same pass/fail verdict.”

    Think deeper: A description is a contract with a component you don’t own and can’t pin: the vendor’s model decides the routing, and it can change next month. Which of your usual contract-testing habits still apply here, and which rely on something you no longer have?

    How good does routing have to be, skill by skill?

    The pattern

    A classifier with a service level, like a fraud rule or a spam filter. Nobody asks those to be perfect. You decide which error you can live with and tune towards it. Routing rules on an integration platform are the nearest thing you’ve already run, except that those do exactly what you wrote.

    What is really being decided

    Whether every skill needs the same bar, and who sets it. A read-only reviewer that fires by mistake wastes a minute. A skill that sends or changes something and fires by mistake can do harm. For those, the safer choice may be not to let it fire by itself at all: Claude Code has disable-model-invocation: true, and Codex has an allow_implicit_invocation setting.

    The forces

    • Broad against narrow: a wider description misses less and fires wrongly more. You usually trade one for the other.
    • A shared budget: Claude Code’s listing scales at 1% of the context window and drops descriptions “starting with the skills you invoke least” when it overflows. Codex defaults to 2%, or 8,000 characters. Our reading: someone else’s new skill could change whether yours fires.
    • Coarse measures: with three runs, a request’s rate can only be 0, 33, 67 or 100%. That’s fine for spotting failures, and poor for comparing two good descriptions.
    • Test effort: 20 requests, three runs, two versions is 120 fresh chats. By hand that takes a group, or it needs automation.

    Left open

    • Who sets the bar for a skill: its author, its users or whoever carries the risk?
    • Should a skill that can change things ever fire without being asked?
    • When someone adds a skill, whose routing tests should run again?
    How to improve a description without fooling yourself

    The method in this step comes from the open standard’s guide: “about 20 queries: 8-10 that should trigger and 8-10 that shouldn’t”, three runs as “a reasonable starting point”, and 0.5 as “a reasonable default” threshold. It calls near misses the most valuable negatives: requests “that share keywords or concepts with your skill but actually need something different”.

    To improve a description, it splits the requests about 60% to 40%, shuffled once and kept fixed. You edit using train failures only, pick the best round by validation score (“Five iterations is usually enough”), then finish on 5 to 10 fresh requests. Anthropic’s skill-creator runs the same kind of loop where it has the tools, in Claude Code. In Claude chat it can’t, because the loop needs claude -p.

    Length limits differ. The specification and claude.ai allow 1,024 characters. Claude Code truncates the combined description and when_to_use at 1,536 in its listing. Codex states no limit per description. To stay portable, write to 1,024 and put the key use case first.

    Vendors also disagree on style. Agent Skills says to use the imperative and to err on the side of being pushy. Anthropic’s best practices say to write in the third person. Neither is universal, which is one more reason to test.

    With or without

    A skill has to beat something. Run the same tasks with it and with no skill at all, on the same model.

    Step5.3

    Part 5
    Evaluate a skill
    Time
    15 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    Ask for predictions before anyone runs a task. Many people assume any skill beats none, so ask what would change their mind. Pair people now, because each will score the other’s outputs in step 5.4. Watch for people continuing an old chat: every run needs a new one.

    You know roughly when it fires. Now the question people tend to skip: when it does fire, is the answer better than what the assistant would have given anyway? General assistants already know a fair amount about data modelling. A skill only earns its place through the difference.

    Run each task twice

    This step tests what the skill does once it’s running, so select it directly. Versions A and B have the same body, so either will do. Keep both chats for each task, because you’ll need the outputs in the next step. In a group you’ll be handing them to a partner.

    • With the skill: new chat, select it with @entity-definition-review, then send the task.
    • No skill: new chat, no @. ChatGPT can still use a relevant skill automatically, so check for the fingerprint from step 5.2. If it appears, the run isn’t a baseline. Take the skill out, or use the option your workspace gives you, and run it again.
    • Comparing: by hand. We found no comparison feature in OpenAI’s docs that we could read.

    Checked 7 November 2026; confirm in your own workspace.

    • With the skill: new chat with the skill on. Send the task and check it loaded. If it didn’t, start a new chat and ask for entity-definition-review by name.
    • No skill: turn it off with its toggle in Customize > Skills, then start a new chat. Anthropic’s support article says disabled skills “won’t be available to Claude”.
    • Comparing: by hand for now. skill-creator in Claude chat runs test prompts one at a time and skips the baseline. Cowork and Claude Code add one for you, with pass rates, timing and tokens. You’ll compare with those in step 5.5.

    Checked 7 November 2026.

    No skills feature? Paste the whole skill at the top of a new chat for the “with” arm, and use a plain new chat for the other. That compares the instructions fairly, since this step doesn’t test firing. Working alone, run Tasks 1 and 2 and record it as a rough check.

    Review this entity definition: Enrolment: The record in the student system that shows which course a student is on. Review this entity definition and give me the version to use: Visiting Scholar: Someone from another university who is here for a while. Review this entity definition: Supervisors: A supervisor is a staff member who supervises research students, with their name, staff number and faculty.
    If you have time: cut it in half

    Download the skill and delete whatever you think earns nothing. Aim for about half its length. Install or paste your shorter copy, run Tasks 1 and 3 again in new chats, and compare.

    Think deeper: The baseline isn’t fixed. Each model upgrade raises what “no skill” can do, so a skill that beat it in March may add nothing by November, with no change on your side. How would you find out, and would you be willing to retire something people have grown used to? Also: what if a skill doesn’t beat no skill on quality but makes every review come out in the same format? Is that enough?

    What should a skill have to beat?

    The pattern

    A control group, or the “do nothing” option in a business case. A proposal that never states the alternative can’t show a benefit. The same goes for a skill.

    What is really being decided

    Whether a skill gets to exist because someone wrote it, or because it beat the alternative. And which alternative: no skill for a new one, the previous version for an edit. Agent Skills suggests both, snapshotting the old version as the baseline for an existing skill.

    The forces

    • A moving baseline: vendor upgrades improve the “no skill” arm for free, and that may quietly erase a skill’s advantage.
    • Consistency against quality: a skill may not beat no skill on any single answer, and still be worth having because every answer has the same shape and cites the same rules.
    • Upkeep: a skill costs context on every chat and attention whenever it changes, so a tie isn’t free.
    • Cost of proof: a baseline doubles the runs. For a low-stakes skill, it might be more than the decision deserves.

    Left open

    • Should a skill that ties with no skill be retired, or kept for consistency?
    • Which of your skills would you least want to see compared with no skill?
    • Who checks again after a model upgrade, and does anyone tell them it happened?
    What the benchmarks found, and how paired runs work

    SkillsBench (Li et al., 2026, preprint) ran 87 tasks across 18 model and harness configurations. Curated skills raised the average pass rate from 33.9% to 50.5%, with configurations ranging from +4.1 to +25.7 points. On 13 of 87 tasks the effect was negative, down to −7.4 points. By length: compact +19.0, standard +21.5, detailed +14.5, comprehensive +0.7. That bears on the cut test above, though the authors also ask whether gains “could partly reflect ‘more context’”.

    SWE-Skills-Bench (Han et al., 2026, preprint) ran 98 skills on 10 requirements each. It reports that “92 of 98 skills have no statistically significant effect”, with a pass ratio of 76.59% to 76.93%; 4 skills helped clearly and 2 did harm. Read it precisely: “Ineffective means that no directional effect was detected with ten requirements, not that the effect is zero.” Requirements were built from the skills themselves, and each task ran once each way.

    ACES (Kevin et al., 2026, preprint) reports positive lift in 689 of 947 paired cases, or 72.8%. That’s a composite that includes process measures, from clustered cases on 58 production skills, so it isn’t 947 independent skills.

    How to run pairs properly. Agent Skills: “run each test case twice: once with the skill and once without it (or with a previous version).” Each run starts with a clean context, using subagents or a separate session. Record total_tokens and duration_ms as well, because a skill that gives the same answer for twice the tokens has still lost. Standard deviation “is only meaningful with multiple runs per eval”, which is why one run per arm is only a direction.

    Score it blind

    Turn vague opinions into pass or fail checks, agree on one example, then score outputs without knowing which is which.

    Step5.4

    Part 5
    Evaluate a skill
    Time
    15 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    The calibration example is the heart of this step. Make people mark it separately and compare before anyone explains. When a pair disagrees, don’t settle it for them: ask whether the check is vague or whether they want different things. Both are useful findings.

    You have a first impression from step 5.3. It’s probably influenced by knowing which output came from the skill, and by which one is longer or tidier. Now you’ll set it aside.

    1 Fix these checks

    Here are three checks someone might write for this skill. Rewrite one so that two people who know the subject would mark it the same way without talking.

    • The review is helpful.
    • The rewrite is clear and professional.
    • Rate the quality from 1 to 5.
    One way to fix them

    Pass or fail is practitioner advice, not a tested result. Husain and Shankar’s evals FAQ says “Binary evaluations force clearer thinking and more consistent labeling”, and we found no comparative study behind it. Agent Skills adds a useful habit: “Require concrete evidence for a PASS.” Note the words that earned it.

    2 Agree on one example

    Mark this output for Task 2 against the three checks below, separately, then compare with a partner. If you’re alone, write your marks down before opening the answer.

    **Visiting Scholar** – Needs rework

| Check         | Problem                                  | Fix                               |
|---------------|------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| Clear meaning | “Here” and “for a while” are vague.      | Say where and for roughly how long. |
| Distinct      | Could also describe an exchange student. | Say what sets it apart.           |

**Rewritten:** A Visiting Scholar is an academic from another university who is hosted here for a limited period.

**Questions:** What sets a Visiting Scholar apart from an exchange student?
    1. Names “here” or “for a while” as too vague
    2. Asks at least one question about what is missing
    3. The rewrite adds no fact missing from the request

    Illustrative. Adapted from real output by a model in our own dry run, shortened for this exercise.

    How we marked it

    1: pass, and it’s quotable. 2: pass, for the same reason. 3: we marked fail, and we expect some of you won’t have. “Limited period” is just rewording “for a while”. But “academic” narrows who counts, and the request didn’t say that. “Hosted” is closer, and we could be argued out of it.

    If you and your partner split on check 3, that’s the exercise working. The check looked sharp until someone had to apply it. So write down what you’ll count: the task sheet below lists a length of time, a rule, an owner, a sponsor, a status, a purpose or a relationship. Add “or who counts” if that’s the rule you both want. Then apply it to everything.

    This comes from rater training in performance appraisal, where frame-of-reference training, which agrees what good looks like before people rate, “is an effective method of improving rating accuracy” (Roch et al., 2012, abstract only). Applying it to scoring AI output is our inference.

    3 Score the outputs

    In a pair: swap devices. Paste your outputs into your partner’s page, click the shuffle button yourself, and hand it back without saying which is which. They score, you do the same for theirs. Hand over the task sheet too.

    Alone: paste and shuffle them yourself. This is less blind: you ran those chats and may recognise them, and length or format can give them away. Leave a gap before you score if you can, and write the limit next to your result.

    The task sheet, with all the checks

    Task 1: the stored record

  • Says the definition describes a stored record or a system, not the business thing
  • The rewrite does not mention a record, a system or a database
  • The rewrite adds no fact missing from the request
    •

    Task 2: the missing facts

  • Names “here” or “for a while” as too vague
  • Asks at least one question about what is missing
  • The rewrite adds no fact missing from the request
    •

    Task 3: several plain faults

  • Flags the plural name
  • Flags the circular wording
  • Flags name, staff number and faculty as attributes
    •

    Nothing leaves your browser. Results are included in your exported notes.

    4 Read what the scores tell you

    • Checks that passed in both arms tell you nothing about the skill. Agent Skills says to remove them, because they “inflate the with-skill pass rate”. Task 3 may be all of this. If so, you’ve learned that those checks can’t justify the skill.
    • Checks that failed in both arms show a gap the skill isn’t closing.
    • Compare with your first impression. Did the one that looked better score better?

    Think deeper: Two senior architects disagree on a check, and rewording doesn’t help. One thinks a definition should mention lifecycle, and the other thinks that belongs elsewhere. Is that a faulty check, or a real difference in what your practice believes? Who should settle it, and what should happen to the view that loses? If a skill then enforces one side, has it just made an architecture decision?

    Who gets to say what good means?

    The pattern

    Segregation of duties, plus double marking. Auditors don’t audit their own work, and exam boards mark samples twice to find where the marking scheme is unclear. Anthropic’s enterprise guide says it directly: “Skill authors should not be their own reviewers.”

    What is really being decided

    Two separate things that are easy to run together: who sets the standard, and who applies it. Writing the checks is a decision about what your practice values. Applying them ought to be close to clerical. If it isn’t, the checks need work.

    The forces

    • One owner against many voices: Husain and Shankar say that “For most small to medium-sized companies, appointing a single domain expert as a ‘benevolent dictator’ is the most effective approach.” That’s practitioner judgement. Aroyo and Welty (2015) count “Disagreement Is Bad” and “One Is Enough” among the myths of annotation, in a medical setting with crowd workers. Our reading: one owner decides what good means, and a panel finds what they missed.
    • Independence against headcount: two scorers per output cost twice as much, and a small team may not have an independent person to spare.
    • A model as scorer: cheap and tireless, and it needs checking itself (see Going deeper).
    • Tacit standards: writing checks forces your practice’s unwritten rules into the open, and some people won’t want that.

    Left open

    • Who owns the definition of good for a skill your whole practice shares?
    • How independent is independent enough, in a small team?
    • When should a disagreement be recorded rather than resolved?
    Calibration, criteria drift and using a model as judge

    Checks change as you score. Shankar et al. (2024, nine practitioners, on eval tools rather than skills) describe criteria drift: “users need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs helps users define criteria”. Agent Skills reaches the same place in practice, adding assertions after the first outputs because “you often don’t know what ‘good’ looks like until the skill has run”. That creates a real tension with blind scoring. A check written after seeing outputs can quietly favour one arm. Our reading: write checks from a practice task, then freeze them before the scored round. This step’s checks came from our own dry run, so they weren’t written in advance either.

    Independent first. Husain and Shankar: “Have annotators label the same examples independently before they discuss them.” LangSmith and Braintrust both build review tools that hide other reviewers’ marks. Those are product features, not evidence that blind review improves outcomes.

    Mechanical before model. Agent Skills says a script is “more reliable than LLM judgment” for mechanical checks. Anthropic: “deterministic graders where possible, LLM graders where necessary”. “Does the rewrite contain the word record?” needs no judge.

    Model judges have known biases. Zheng et al. (NeurIPS 2023) showed position bias and verbosity bias. GPT-4 and people agreed on 85% of non-tie votes, and 66% with ties counted. Panickssery et al. (NeurIPS 2024, abstract only) report that evaluators can score their own outputs higher, in the way the abstract defines self-preference. So give a judge a shuffled pair if you use one, and don’t have the same model mark its own work without checking. Agent Skills suggests blind comparison with an LLM judge as an optional tip when comparing two versions.

    Build your eval kit

    Use a skill that writes test plans, see which planted flaws it finds, then give your verdict and adapt the kit to your own work.

    Step5.5

    Part 5
    Evaluate a skill
    Time
    15 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    Take the second show of hands before you open the answer key, and put it next to the first count. Ask who changed their mind, and which result changed it. Name the trap out loud: a kit written by a model tests what a model thinks matters, so people’s own failures have to go in.

    You’ve done it by hand. It took a lot of chats, and you had to invent the requests, tasks and checks. Most of that planning can be packaged as a skill. The running and deciding shouldn’t be.

    1 Run the kit on the skill you’ve been testing

    Install it the way you installed the last one, naming the folder skill-eval-kit. No skills feature? Paste the whole kit at the top of a new chat. Before you run it, predict: which faults will it find, and which will it miss?

    Write a test plan for the skill below. I have no real failures yet. [PASTE THE WHOLE OF VERSION A FROM STEP 5.1 HERE]

    2 Give your verdict

    Now use what you measured. This rule is in the kit, so you can use it again.

    VerdictWhen
    KeepIt meets both trigger minimums, passes more checks than no skill on at least one task, and is worse on none.
    FixIt fails in a way you can trace to a line. Wrong firing means the description. Right firing with a wrong result means the instructions. Fix it and run the tests again.
    RetireAfter one round of fixes, it still doesn’t beat no skill on any check that can differ.

    This rule is our suggestion, not a standard. Change it if your context calls for a different one, but change it before you run the tests.

    3 Open the answer key

    The planted flaws, and how the kit did

    We built this skill to be faulty, starting from the one in Part 2. Don’t use it for real work.

    FlawWhat we changedWhat should expose it
    1 · Vague descriptionNo clear trigger and no “not for” line.The trigger test: near misses about physical design
    2 · Free to inventRemoved “Do not add facts”, “ask for one and stop”, the Questions line and “adds no new facts”. Added “complete and ready to paste”, which sounds like a virtue.With or without, and the check “adds no fact missing from the request”
    3 · Lost gotchasRemoved the Gotchas section, so nothing says to flag “the record in the system”. Softened check 2 to “Clear meaning”.With or without, and the Task 1 checks
    4 · PaddingAdded three sections and an opening line telling the model what it already knows.Cutting it in half

    Score the kit’s plan against them:

    What we saw in a rough dry run. One run per cell, on one Claude Sonnet model through an agent tool rather than a chat product, scored by the writer and not blind. Treat it as a check on these materials, not a result. Yours count for more.

    Checks passedFlawed skillNo skillSound original
    Task 12 of 31 of 33 of 3
    Task 21 of 31 of 32 of 3

    Two things stood out. Flaw 3 didn’t show: all three flagged the stored record, even with the gotcha gone. On that run, the gotcha added nothing the model didn’t already know, and an older or smaller model might behave differently. That’s why you test rather than assume. Flaw 2 did show: the flawed skill and no skill both wrote in durations, purposes and rules nobody had supplied, while the sound original asked questions. On Task 2, the flawed skill was no better than having no skill at all.

    In our one dry run of the kit, the plan found flaws 1, 2 and 4, and had no check aimed at flaw 3. It can’t see what was taken out. Its “What is missing” section helps, but only your own failures can tell it what went wrong before.

    Try the fix: run the sound original on Task 2

    This is what “fix it and run the tests again” looks like. Install or paste this version, run Task 2 in a new chat, and mark it with the same checks.

    The trap. A kit written by a model tests what a model thinks matters. It’s a good first draft of a test plan, and it knows nothing about the mistakes your reviewers keep correcting. Those are the tests worth having, so add them first. Keep real data out of your prompts unless your organisation approves.

    4 Adapt it to your own work

    Pick a skill you use or plan to share, or a prompt you keep reusing. Run the kit on it, and give it one real failure.

    OpenAI’s developer docs give a five-part test list. The kit covers all five, and adds what the list doesn’t have: a baseline, repeat runs and grading.

    OpenAI’s listIn the kit
    Direct requests that should activate itShould-fire requests
    Indirect requests with the same goalShould-fire requests, in varied wording
    Incomplete inputs that should prompt a follow-up questionA task with something missing, and a check for the question
    Requests that should not activate itNear misses
    Edge cases where it must not invent or overstepThe task that tempts it to break its own rules

    OpenAI’s advice on what to change matches the verdict rule: the description if it fires at the wrong time, the instructions if it picks the right workflow but gives inconsistent results.

    Checked 7 November 2026.

    If you have Cowork or Claude Code, compare your hand results with skill-creator’s benchmark. It adds a no-skill baseline, parallel runs, pass rates, timing and tokens. In Claude chat it doesn’t: it runs prompts one at a time and skips those parts. Custom skills don’t sync between claude.ai and Claude Code, so in Claude Code put a copy of the skill folder in ~/.claude/skills/ first.

    /plugin install skill-creator@claude-plugins-official evaluate my entity-definition-review skill with skill-creator

    Compare the results with yours. Did its checks test what yours did? Did it reach the same conclusion? Where they differ, which would you trust, and why? Check your plan, and whether Cowork is available to you.

    Checked 7 November 2026.

    Think deeper: The kit is itself a skill, so by this Part’s logic it should have to beat no skill. What would that test look like? What is the no-skill baseline for writing a test plan, and who is fit to judge a plan: someone who has run one, or the results it goes on to catch? You could run the kit on itself. Would you trust the answer?

    Should skills go through a release gate?

    The pattern

    A conformance gate plus a regression suite, as in continuous integration. The difference is that the component’s behaviour can change with nothing committed on your side, so a gate triggered only by your own changes won’t catch everything.

    What is really being decided

    What evidence a skill needs before it’s shared, who runs the tests again after a vendor model update, and who may retire a skill. The third is the one most organisations won’t have an answer for, and it’s where a catalogue either stays useful or fills up.

    The forces

    • Rigour against pace: skills are quick to write. A heavy gate sends people back to private prompts, which have no gate at all.
    • Consequence: a skill feeding funding or governance work needs more than one drafting a meeting note. A single gate for both will be wrong for one of them.
    • Platform controls aren’t evals: Claude’s Publishing setting can be Requires review, Open or Off, and Enterprise scanning looks for risk, though Anthropic says a pass “isn’t a guarantee”. ChatGPT owners control who can create and share (all checked 7 November 2026). None of these tests whether a skill helps.
    • Who pays: paired runs cost tokens and people’s hours, and the benefit often goes to another team.
    • Retirement: Claude Code’s /skill-doctor flags skills never invoked. Usage isn’t value, but it’s a start, and we found no equivalent documented for ChatGPT on the pages we could read.

    Left open

    • What is the least evidence you’d accept before a skill reaches the whole practice?
    • Who hears about a vendor’s model change, and whose job is it to rerun the tests?
    • Who has the authority to retire a skill that a senior colleague likes?
    Automating it: claude plugin eval and OpenAI’s Codex method

    claude plugin eval

    Requires Claude Code v2.1.269 or later, and targets a plugin directory with a manifest or a skills-directory plugin. claude plugin eval init proposes cases and graders. Each case runs “three times by default” per arm, with the plugin and with no plugin, and Δ is the difference. As the docs put it, “If a case scores 1.0 both with and without the plugin, the plugin isn’t what made it pass.”

    There are six grader types: regex, tool_used, tool_order, file_exists, llm and baseline. The first four cost nothing, and an llm grader passes on at least two of three judge votes. tool_used: Skill is left out of the score in two-arm runs because it would inflate Δ, and shows as an indicator only. So this measures whether a skill helps more directly than whether it fires.

    Each case is “a real model call on your account”. --max-cost-usd sets a ceiling, and --ablation none halves the cost by dropping the baseline, along with the comparison that gives the method its point. Its suites and skill-creator’s evals/evals.json aren’t interchangeable: “neither tool reads the other’s case files”. /skill-doctor (v2.1.252 or later) reports what each skill costs and how often it’s used.

    OpenAI’s Codex method

    Not available to everyone yet. Codex is a separate product, and many organisations don’t offer it to staff yet. Read this for orientation, and don’t plan a session around it unless your group has access.

    OpenAI’s blog post defines success first (outcome, process, style and efficiency), then builds a CSV of prompts with id, should_trigger and prompt. codex exec --json gives a JSONL trace, which deterministic checks can read, for example that a command ran and exited 0, or that a file exists. A second, read-only codex exec grades against a rubric through --output-schema.

    It has no no-skill baseline and no repeat runs. The only comparison is the negative control, so add both if you use it. And check the flags: the post still shows --full-auto, while OpenAI’s current docs say it’s no longer supported and point to --sandbox workspace-write. By default, codex exec runs in a read-only sandbox.

    Read more

    • Claude Code: plugin evals
    • Claude Code: plugins CLI reference
    • Anthropic: creating and running skills, by surface
    • OpenAI: Testing Agent Skills Systematically with Evals
    • OpenAI: non-interactive mode
    • OpenAI: build skills, including the five-part test list
    Retired tools: don’t build on these

    The OpenAI Evals platform. OpenAI’s deprecations page says existing evals became read-only on 31 October 2026, and that the dashboard and API are scheduled to shut down on 30 November 2026. The v1/prompts API and Agent Builder share that date. The page points to a migration guide named “Moving from OpenAI Evals to Promptfoo”, which we have not read. This is separate from the Codex method above, which doesn’t use that platform.

    The old Claude Workbench. A notice of 17 July 2026 said access would end on 17 August 2026, and that saved prompts, variables and evals would not carry over. By 18 August the release notes said “Workbench is now playground in the Claude Console”. Its help page says playground “does not support saving prompt history or evaluating prompts”. So the Console has no eval tool to learn.

    One more stale line to watch for: Anthropic’s authoring best practices still say “There is not currently a built-in way to run these evaluations.” For Claude Code, that’s been overtaken by the tools in the panel above.

    Read more

    • OpenAI: deprecations
    • Anthropic: release notes
    • Anthropic: how to use the playground
    • Anthropic: skill authoring best practices

    What you can do now

    • Test firing in both directions, with near misses, and report a number.
    • Set up a fair comparison against no skill.
    • Write checks that can be marked pass or fail, and score without knowing which output is which.
    • Give a verdict of keep, fix or retire, and name the result that decided it.

    The rest of this series uses this method: from step 6.1 on, each skill you build gets tested the same way.

    Why an if-then plan? A meta-analysis of 94 tests found d = .65 for plans in this form (Gollwitzer and Sheeran, 2006), and a later one of 642 tests found .27 ≤ d ≤ .66 depending on the outcome (Sheeran et al., 2024). We read both as abstracts only, and neither studied architects. 2006 · 2024

  • I added at least one real failure of my own to the kit.

    Start from a bad draft

    Mark up an ADR drafted with no skill, trace its claims back to the brief, then see what your own assistant does with one line.

    Step6.1

    Part 6
    Skills that draft
    Time
    15 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    Give eight quiet minutes for the mark-up before anyone opens the answers. If the room starts arguing about whether a shared service is right, park it: the brief has already decided that. The argument to have here is about the record.

    An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) gets read years later, by people who can’t ask you what you meant. Equal Experts, who generate ADRs with AI tools, put the risk plainly: “If they’re wrong, they quickly become noise and can mislead future team members.” So before building anything, find out what wrong looks like.

    Mark up the draft

    Westmere University is fictional, and three of its projects want to answer policy questions. You don’t need Part 4 for this, although the decision will look familiar if you did step 4.6. Here is what the author was given.

    And here is the draft that came back. We wrote it for this course as a composite of known failure patterns, so no model produced these exact words. You’ll get a real one in a few minutes.

    Read it as if it had landed in your review queue. Hold the brief next to it and check every claim, reference and number. Write down what you would send back, and anything you’d leave alone.

    The answers – open them after you’ve written yours

    Now score yourself. Record whether you flagged each one. The last three are traps: reasonable things that a reviewer on autopilot might also strike.

    The eleven faults fall into four kinds, and you’ll meet these again:

    • Invented: facts, sources and reasons nobody supplied. The Hallworth link ends in .example, a domain reserved for examples, so it can’t resolve. A real invented link might land on a page that looks right.
    • Dropped: the awkward parts. The 38 restricted documents, the cost ceiling, the deadline and the funded-owner rule have all gone, and the decision looks easier without them.
    • Decided for you: “should be approved” isn’t the author’s call.
    • Padded: sentences that would fit any decision at any university.

    So what: Look at what you missed. A reviewer with ten of these to get through will miss at least that, and the draft’s confident, finished tone makes it easier to do so.

    Now get a real one

    Our draft is a composite, so test whether the pattern holds on your own assistant. Open a fresh chat, with memory off if you can. Westmere is invented, so this is safe to paste. Don’t try it on real work unless your organisation approves.

    Predict first: given only one line, will it ask you for the missing drivers and sources, or fill them in?

    Write an Architecture Decision Record for this decision: Westmere University will run one shared service for answering policy questions, instead of each project building its own.

    A good answer asks first. If yours cited real pages from a web search, they’re still not Westmere’s sources. It may also have done better than our composite, and that’s worth knowing too: you’re measuring your assistant, not confirming our story.

    Equal Experts report the same failure from practice: their tools “frequently hallucinated reference material, including non-existent APIs, web pages, or entire product features”. That is practitioner experience, not a measurement. Writing about agents that build systems, Poort of CGI says they “fill in missing decisions themselves with implicit assumptions” (translated from Dutch; an opinion piece, with no data). Our reading: a drafting model does the same thing to a document, and that’s why the skill you build in step 6.4 has to stop and ask.

    In a group session, compare mark-ups. The faults only one person caught are the ones to discuss.

    Think deeper: This draft reaches the conclusion the brief wanted. Would you have checked the Hallworth figure as hard if it had argued for the option you opposed? What should a review board do differently when a generated record tells it what it already hoped to hear?

    What does one unchecked record do to a decision log?

    The pattern

    Data quality at the point of entry, and lineage. You already know that a bad value in master data gets copied faster than it gets corrected. A decision log is a small master-data store: later records and business cases cite it as fact.

    What is really being decided

    What a record has to show before it enters the log, whether generated records meet the same bar as hand-written ones, and whether anyone can later tell which entries were checked, and against what.

    The forces

    • Speed against trust: Equal Experts write that they “might generate dozens of ADRs in a single morning”. Their case is retrospective records of decisions already made, with no measurements. The volume is plausible, but the reading time doesn’t shrink to match.
    • Polish against substance: a tidy document looks reviewed. Format used to be weak evidence of care, and now it’s no evidence at all.
    • Cost of correction: fixing a wrong figure costs little before acceptance. After three records cite it, it’s a small investigation.
    • Backfill against new decisions: reconstructing old decisions has a different risk from recording new ones, because nobody may remember well enough to catch an invented reason.

    Left open

    • If you found one invented figure in an accepted ADR, what would you do about every record that cites it?
    • Should generated records be marked as generated in the log, and would that change how anyone reads them?
    • Is correcting an accepted record an edit, or a new decision that supersedes it?
    Three ways a reference can be wrong

    Invented. NIST calls this confabulation: “confidently stated but erroneous or false content”, and warns that outputs may include “confabulated logic or citations that purport to justify or explain the system’s answer”. Its suggested action is plain: “Review and verify sources and citations in GAI system outputs”.

    Unsupported. The source exists but doesn’t say that. ALCE (Gao et al., EMNLP 2023) found that on the ELI5 dataset “even the best models lack complete citation support 50% of the time”. Read that carefully: it measures statements their cited passages don’t fully support, not invented references. The models are from 2023, and the questions aren’t about architecture.

    Misapplied. The source exists and says it, but about a different context. We found no measurement of this for ADRs. It’s our own category, and it’s the one a tool is least likely to catch.

    Guardrails help but don’t close the gap. Equal Experts add rules such as “References MUST exist – check each reference to ensure that the link is valid”, and say these “still won’t be foolproof”. Step 11.2 comes back to checking citations against live sources.

    Read more

    • NIST AI 600-1: Generative AI Profile (2024)
    • Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations (Gao et al., EMNLP 2023)
    • Accelerating ADRs with Generative AI (Louw, Hmeid and Brabban, Equal Experts, 2025)
    • LLM09:2025 Misinformation, including overreliance (OWASP)

  • I gave my own assistant one line and noted whether it asked or filled in the gaps.
  • I can name the four kinds of fault: invented, dropped, decided for you and padded.

    Anchor it on a template

    A template fixes the form of a draft and leaves its facts untouched. Predict how much of the bad draft it would have stopped.

    Step6.2

    Part 6
    Skills that draft
    Time
    10 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    Keep this one quick. If someone’s organisation uses another format, let them keep it: the argument holds for any format, as long as they can say which parts are required. The surprise to protect is how little the template stops, so collect predictions first.

    Ask for “a good ADR” and the model decides what an ADR is. A template takes that choice away. The Agent Skills guidance calls this calibrating control: “Match the specificity of your instructions to the fragility of the task.” The form of a record that a board reads every week is fragile, so fix it.

    We use MADR 4.0 because it’s specific and its licence lets us reuse it: “dual-licensed under MIT and CC0”. MADR doesn’t label sections as required. It marks some as optional, and only four parts are left unmarked. Everything else, including the status line, is yours to require or not.

    Predict

    In step 6.1 you found eleven faults. If the author had been handed this template and nothing else, how many of the eleven would it have stopped?

    Our answer – open it after you’ve predicted
    FaultWhat stops it
    No options consideredTemplate: Considered Options is core
    Padding and an executive summaryTemplate: there’s nowhere to put them
    Invented Hallworth referenceHouse rule: supplied sources only
    “Should be approved”, no statusHouse rule: status is proposed, and a person signs
    Strategy 2030, “extensive experience”Gotcha: cite only what you were given
    “Changes constantly”Gotcha: copy numbers exactly
    Permissions waved away; cost and date goneGotcha: keep every driver
    No funded ownerGotcha: check earlier decisions
    Generic risksGotcha: list a real “Bad, because”

    Those nine rows cover the eleven faults: the fifth row holds two, and the seventh holds two.

    So what: A template fixes the form and leaves the facts alone. A filled-in slot looks complete whether or not anything in it is true, which can make an invented reason harder to spot.

    Read the same decision on the template

    Here is the same decision, written by hand for this course. Read it next to the bad draft.

    Write your house rules

    MADR says nothing about your board. What must a record in your organisation have that the template doesn’t ask for? A review forum, a risk reference and a superseded-by link are typical. Write down two or three. You’ll add them to the skill in step 6.4.

    Where the template lives

    Put the template inside SKILL.md, as the worked skill does. OpenAI documents optional folders in a skill, but we couldn’t confirm how a bundled reference file loads in ChatGPT chat. If you want a separate file, test it: ask the skill to state the third heading of its template. Checked 7 November 2026; confirm in your own workspace.

    Either works. Anthropic’s how-to says “the skill’s whole folder, scripts included, is copied into the code execution sandbox”, so a separate template file can sit beside SKILL.md. Inside SKILL.md is the portable choice, and that’s what the worked skill does. Checked 7 November 2026.

    Think deeper: MADR says the number of options “can vary”. Our house rule says two or more. An obliging model can meet that rule by inventing a second option to lose. Which of your own house rules can be met on paper without being met in fact? And what should a record say when only one option was ever viable?

    Whose template is the standard, and who may change it?

    The pattern

    A paved road on top of a pinned dependency. You don’t fork the standard for every project. You pin a version, publish what your organisation adds, and make the supported route the easiest one to take.

    What is really being decided

    Once a skill writes the records, the template in the skill is the standard in practice, whatever the wiki says. So the decision is who owns that copy, how a change to it gets approved, and what happens to the records already written on the old one.

    The forces

    • Comparability against fit: one format makes records easy to search and compare, and fits no team exactly.
    • Licences: MADR is MIT or CC0. arc42’s template is CC BY-SA 4.0: you may adapt it inside your organisation without publishing, but a published adaptation must carry the same licence. Nygard’s post shows no licence, so describe the format and don’t copy the post.
    • Upgrades: a new upstream version is a change to every skill built on it, and some teams will have copied the old one.
    • Ceremony: each required section adds reading time. A section nobody reads is a cost with no return.

    Left open

    • Who can approve a change to the template inside a skill that several teams use?
    • When the template changes, do old records get migrated, or does the log hold two formats for good?
    • Which sections would you remove if the board could only read one page?
    Three formats, and what the evidence does and doesn’t say

    Constraining the form. Anthropic’s authoring guide calls this setting “appropriate degrees of freedom”, from high (text instructions) to low (specific scripts). A template is low freedom for structure and high freedom for wording. The Agent Skills guidance adds “Provide defaults, not menus”: give one template, not a choice of three.

    Studies of generated ADRs. Dhar et al. (ICSA 2024, 95 ADRs) found that GPT-4 with no examples generates “relevant and accurate Design Decisions, although they fall short of human-level performance”. DRAFT (Dhar et al., preprint, 2025, 4,911 ADRs) reports that it “outperforms all other approaches in effectiveness”, but it combines few-shot examples, retrieval and fine-tuning. Our reading: fine-tuning isn’t a step most teams would take for a skill, so don’t read that result as “a template plus examples is enough”. Neither study tests a template on its own.

    Completeness isn’t quality. Iasa’s BTABoK MCP server offers a check_completeness tool that will “Check a filled in artifact against its schema and say what is missing.” That’s useful, and it checks only that the slots are filled. Step 10.3 builds the same kind of check for your ADRs, and step 7.1 sorts what such a check can and can’t see.

    Read more

    • Can LLMs Generate Architectural Design Decisions? (Dhar et al., ICSA 2024)
    • DRAFT-ing Architectural Design Decisions using LLMs (Dhar et al., preprint, 2025)
    • Skill authoring best practices (Anthropic)
    • BTABoK MCP server (Iasa Global)

    Harvest the gotchas

    Turn twenty invented reviewer comments into a short list of gotchas, and work out which comments shouldn't become rules at all.

    Step6.3

    Part 6
    Skills that draft
    Time
    15 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    Silent sorting first, then compare. The useful arguments are about the comments that shouldn’t become rules, especially C19 and C20. In a group, ask two people who sorted a comment differently to explain why.

    You now have the form. What makes this author yours is what your reviewers keep having to say. The Agent Skills guidance puts it this way: “The highest-value content in many skills is a list of gotchas — environment-specific facts that defy reasonable assumptions.” And it gives the method: “When an agent makes a mistake you have to correct, add the correction to the gotchas section.” That’s guidance from people who write skills, not a measured result, but you can test it in step 6.5.

    Sort the comments

    These comments on four earlier drafts are invented. Not all of them should change the skill.

    Predict: how many of the twenty should reach the gotcha list, and how many gotchas will they make? Then sort them, and write your gotchas. For each candidate, ask three questions:

    1. Would the model do this again if nobody told it not to? If it would follow the instruction anyway, the line is wasted.
    2. Could someone see whether it held? “Be accurate” fails. “Every [S…] is on the supplied list” passes.
    3. Did it recur, or is it costly when missed? One comment can be enough if the error is serious.
    The worked set – open it after you’ve written yours

    We got fourteen comments into nine gotchas, with six comments going elsewhere.

    CommentsGoes to
    C1, C6Gotcha: cite only what you were given
    C3, C11Gotcha: “because” must use the drivers
    C7, C16Gotcha: keep every driver, especially the awkward ones
    C12, C17Gotcha: no straw men
    C4, C13Gotcha: copy numbers exactly, and show any sum
    C8Gotcha: check earlier decisions you were given
    C18Gotcha: list at least one real “Bad, because”
    C14Gotcha: never set the status to accepted, and leave decision-makers empty
    C5Gotcha: keep it short enough to read in five minutes
    C9Template: the headings are a form problem
    C15Script: a machine can check a status against a list (step 10.3)
    C19People: one reviewer’s view on the decision. It’s a real challenge, and it belongs in the review
    C20People: nothing written down says so, which is why a person has to raise it
    C2, C10People: a one-off typo, and a request for padding that belongs in a handbook

    You can reasonably disagree. “Keep it short” comes from one comment and is the weakest of the nine by our second test, so we kept it only because the chair’s reading time is the real constraint. C8 appears only once, and earns its place on cost.

    WeakStronger
    Be careful with references.Mark every fact with its source ID. If a fact has no source, write “not verified”.
    Give good reasons.“Modern”, “best practice” and “scalable” are not reasons unless a driver says so.
    Consider the downsides.List at least one real “Bad, because”.

    One more check on your reading. The clean ADR in step 6.2 gives 240,000 and 345,000 without showing the sums, so by our own gotcha it should be sent back. We wrote it by hand. Reviewers catch people too.

    Real comments: Reviewer comments often name people, projects and suppliers. Use only what your organisation allows in your AI tool, take out the names, and remember that a gotcha travels with the skill to everyone it’s shared with.

    Think deeper: A harvest only sees what reviewers noticed and bothered to write down. The faults nobody caught never reach it, and one forceful reviewer can turn a preference into a rule for everyone. How would you find the faults your reviewers are missing? And when does a senior architect’s habit deserve to become a gotcha?

    Who owns the loop from correction to rule?

    The pattern

    The post-incident review that feeds a runbook. A failure gets written up without blame, someone decides what changes, and the change is tested. Here the incident is a review comment, the runbook is the gotcha list, and the test is the next run of your eval kit from step 5.5.

    What is really being decided

    Whose judgement gets written into a tool everyone uses. A gotcha quietly turns one review into policy for every later draft, so the decision is who may do that, what evidence they need, and how a rule gets challenged or removed.

    The forces

    • One owner against many reviewers: the tension from step 5.4 applies here too. Aroyo and Welty, working on medical text annotation, found that experts “reach agreement only on 30 percent of the sentences”, so one owner’s list will have gaps that a wider panel can find.
    • Capture against bloat: each rule costs reading time and has to compete with every other rule.
    • Tacit knowledge: a skill keeps some of what a retiring reviewer knew. C20 shows what it can’t keep.
    • Attribution: people comment differently once they know their comments feed a tool, and may stop raising awkward points.

    Left open

    • Who can add a gotcha, and who can remove one that no longer applies?
    • Do reviewers know their comments may become rules, and does that change what they write?
    • How would a team outside architecture dispute a gotcha that affects them?
    How long can a gotcha list get?

    What the numbers say. SkillsBench (Li et al., preprint, v4, 2026) grouped its curated skills by length. Compact skills gained 19.0 points, standard 21.5, detailed 14.5 and comprehensive 0.7. It also reports that “Focused Skills with at most three modules outperform larger or exhaustive bundles.”

    What they don’t say. The groups are different tasks with very different baselines (19.8% to 39.3% with no skills), and comprehensive has only five tasks. So this doesn’t show that shortening a skill would improve it. It’s a reason to test a cut with the method in step 5.3, not a limit to obey. The specification recommends keeping SKILL.md “under 500 lines”, and a body under 5,000 tokens.

    Why harvest instead of writing rules up front. Husain and Shankar call error analysis “the most important activity in evals”. Shankar et al. (2024, a qualitative study of nine practitioners) describe why you can’t skip it: “users need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs helps users define criteria.” The Agent Skills evaluation guide agrees in practice, adding assertions only after the first outputs, because “you often don’t know what ‘good’ looks like until the skill has run.” None of these studied gotchas directly, so applying them here is our reading.

    Read more

    • SkillsBench v4 (Li et al., preprint, 2026)
    • Agent Skills specification and Evaluating skills
    • AI Evals: Everything You Need to Know (Husain and Shankar)
    • Who Validates the Validators? (Shankar et al., 2024)
    • Truth Is a Lie: Crowd Truth and the Seven Myths of Human Annotation (Aroyo and Welty, 2015)

    Build the ADR author

    Make the skill, read every line of it, then check that it stops and asks and that it fires only when it should.

    Step6.4

    Part 6
    Skills that draft
    Time
    15 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    Don’t let installation eat the session. If skills aren’t available, go straight to the paste-in route. In a group, split the trigger table so each person runs a couple of requests, and pool the results. The moment to watch for is someone reading a generated skill and finding a line they didn’t ask for.

    You have a template, house rules and gotchas. Now make them into a skill that writes the decision down and leaves making it to someone else.

    1 Make it

    Choose a route. Asking your assistant to write it shows you what its skill creator adds. Copying the worked skill is quicker. Either way you’ll read every line in the next phase.

    Create a skill called adr-author. It drafts one Architecture Decision Record in MADR 4.0 form from a decision a person has already made. It is not for choosing between options, comparing options without a decision, or reviewing an existing ADR. If the decision, drivers, options or sources are missing, ask once, in one short list, then wait. If no decision has been made, say so and stop. Use these headings exactly: Context and Problem Statement; Decision Drivers; Considered Options; Decision Outcome, with Consequences and Confirmation beneath it; Pros and Cons of the Options; More Information. Put status: proposed, the date and an empty decision-makers line in the front matter. Use these gotchas, word for word: [Paste your gotchas from the harvest step] Add these house rules: [Paste your house rules] Do not add general advice about writing ADRs. Show me every line before installing it.

    Start a new chat with @skill-creator, or use a “Build me a skill” prompt. A draft opens for you to refine, then choose Install. OpenAI lists standalone skills in the desktop app, Codex CLI and IDE extension, and plugin-bundled skills on the web, desktop and mobile. So if you can’t find it on the web, try the desktop app. Availability depends on your plan and workspace settings. Checked 7 November 2026; confirm in your own workspace.

    Find skill-creator under Customize > Skills; skills need code execution switched on. To upload the worked skill instead, ZIP a folder named adr-author with SKILL.md inside it. Anthropic warns that “a SKILL.md sitting at the root of the ZIP isn’t recognized as a skill”. In chat, skill-creator runs test prompts one at a time and skips the no-skill baseline; Cowork and Claude Code add one. In Claude Code, install it with /plugin install skill-creator@claude-plugins-official. Checked 7 November 2026.

    Or start from the worked skill, which already holds the nine gotchas from the worked set. The folder name must match the name line.

    No skills feature? Paste the whole skill at the top of a fresh chat, then add your request below it. That tests the instructions. It can’t test automatic triggering, so skip the trigger test in phase 4 and record that you did.

    Should you trust a generated skill? In SkillsBench (Li et al., preprint, 2026), skills an agent wrote for itself scored 8.1 to 11.5 points below using no skill at all, on all three configurations tried. That doesn’t show AI-written skills are worse. Nobody reviewed those skills or improved them, and the authors say the deficit “mixes content quality with skill-discovery and creator/solver interference effects”. The study didn’t test a draft a person has reviewed, which is what you’re making. So don’t assume either way: read it, then test it. Going deeper below has the details.

    2 Read every line

    Whichever route you took, go through it line by line. Strike anything the model would do anyway (“write clearly”, “be professional”), or anything you can’t trace to a real failure. If a skill creator wrote it, check that your gotchas survived and weren’t softened. Then find one line of the worked skill you’d cut, and defend the cut.

    3 Make it stop

    The riskiest thing this skill can do is carry on. Poort’s warning from step 6.1 is about agents that fill gaps with assumptions, and a cheap, confident draft is a tempting place for that to happen. This skill’s first job is to refuse to guess.

    Predict what each one will do, then run each in its own fresh chat, with the skill selected or pasted in.

    Write an ADR: Westmere University will run one shared service for answering policy questions. We can’t decide between one shared service and letting each project build its own. Write the ADR.

    For Test C, ask it to draft an ADR from the full decision brief.

    If it fails, change one thing and run that test again in a fresh chat, as you did in step 2.5. OpenAI’s checklist gives a good rule for what to change: “Refine the description when the skill activates at the wrong time”, and “Refine the instructions when it chooses the right workflow but produces an inconsistent result.”

    4 Check when it fires

    Use the method from step 5.2. Half of these should fire the skill. The other half are near misses that share its vocabulary, which the skill’s description says to stay out of. Set your minimum first, then run each request in a fresh chat without naming the skill.

    We found no documented sign that a skill fired, so judge by the output: did it use the MADR headings and status: proposed, or ask its short list of questions? Checked 7 November 2026; look for an indicator in your own workspace.

    Anthropic suggests you “review Claude’s thinking to confirm it’s loading the skill”. Check the output as well. Checked 7 November 2026.

    Eight requests run once each are only a rough check. The Agent Skills guidance suggests about 20 requests, three runs each. A miss on a simple request may not mean the description is wrong: the guidance notes a one-step request may not trigger a skill “even if the description matches perfectly”.

    Think deeper: This skill refuses to choose. But someone will type “write it up as the shared service” having given it about ten seconds’ thought, and the skill will produce a confident record of a decision nobody really made. A one-line decision is easy to state and hard to tell from a real one. Can a skill tell the difference? If it can’t, what should stop that record entering your log?

    Who owns a decision when a machine drafted the record?

    The pattern

    Segregation of duties. The person who raises a payment doesn’t approve it. Here, whoever produces the record shouldn’t also be the one who accepts it, and a skill can’t hold accountability at all. Step 5.4 applied the same rule to scoring a skill’s output.

    What is really being decided

    Who counts as the author, and what a reviewer’s signature means. If a person prompts a skill, skims the output and submits it, they’re the author on paper. The decision is what they must have done to deserve that name, and what a reviewer is attesting to: that they checked the sources, that the reasoning holds, or only that they read it.

    The forces

    • Accountability against convenience: a record that’s easy to produce is also easy to submit without owning it.
    • Authority of the output: Poort calls AI “a tool that offers suggestions, first drafts and hypotheses, not an architectural authority”, and notes that “AI-generated output is not automatically evidence” (translated; opinion).
    • Overreliance: OWASP warns of users who “place excessive trust in LLM-generated content, failing to verify its accuracy”. A polished draft invites that.
    • Technical enforcement: an instruction not to set the status is advice to a model. Only a check outside the model can enforce it, which is what step 10.3 adds.

    Left open

    • What must an author have done before their name goes on a generated record?
    • What exactly does your reviewer attest to, and is it written down anywhere?
    • Should the record say a skill drafted it, and which version?
    What the self-generated skills finding does and doesn’t show

    The result. SkillsBench v4 ran 87 tasks in 8 domains, scored by deterministic tests. Compared with no skills, self-generated skills changed the pass rate by −8.1 points on Claude Code with Opus 4.7, −11.3 on Codex with GPT-5.5 and −11.5 on Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Curated skills added +18.2, +19.7 and +24.8 on the same three.

    The method. Each task had two sessions. A creator agent got the task with the curated skills removed and only skill-creator mounted, was told “Do not solve the task directly”, and wrote packs. A fresh solver then ran the task with only those packs. There was no human review, no eval loop and no iteration.

    The confounds, as the authors state them. They retain this arm as “a diagnostic”, outside the main results, and say “its deficit mixes content quality with skill-discovery and creator/solver interference effects.” In the Codex and Gemini family, “10 of 12 audited trajectories never list, read, or mention the generated skills”. That audit picked cases with extreme gaps, so it isn’t a prevalence figure. Claude Code ran at effort max against a baseline at high, and its creator and solver shared one trial context. The authors’ audit also found confidently wrong content in packs that were used.

    What wasn’t tested. AI drafts reviewed by a person, skills improved through evals, and documents judged by reviewers. Our reading: it’s a fair warning against shipping an unread, unreviewed generated skill, and no more than that.
