    Previous step12.3 Stamp the provenance Next step13.1 Define good

    Define good

    Before you compare skills, one named expert decides what passing means. The group’s job is to challenge them.

    Step13.1

    Part 13
    Skills as a team
    Time
    15 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    Choose the expert before the session, and warn them. It must not be the author of a competing skill. When someone asks for a vote, ask who would answer for the result if the vote turned out to be wrong.

    Three colleagues have each written a skill for drafting ADRs, and each prefers their own. All of them are capable, and one is senior. From here on the hard problems are about people, not prompts.

    What the usual signals show

    Popularity data is thin. Zhao et al. (preprint, 2024) found that 90.78% of about 334,000 custom GPTs had no ratings at all. That is a public store, so it says nothing about how good the ratings were or what happens inside an organisation.

    Careful reading is weaker than most of us would like. As step 5.1 showed, ACES (Kevin et al., extended preprint, 2026) found that neither a structural scan nor an LLM judge’s score tracked the lift each skill gave in live runs, with correlations “statistically indistinguishable from zero”. Our reading: you must read a skill to know it is safe, but reading won’t tell you which one works best.

    Find the faults

    A senior colleague proposes this score sheet for the comparison. Find what is wrong with each line before you open the answers.

    1. Overall quality, from 1 to 5.
    2. Uses our MADR template.
    3. Sounds authoritative.
    4. Is comprehensive.
    5. A senior architect would be happy with it.
    6. Everyone on the panel agrees it is good.
    What we would say
    LineThe fault
    1 Quality, 1 to 5Nobody can act on a 3, and two raters’ 3s may mean different things. Husain and Shankar’s view is that “Binary evaluations force clearer thinking and more consistent labeling”. That is practitioner opinion; we found no comparative study.
    2 Uses our templateIt may be a fair rule, but it rules out a differently shaped skill before anything has run. If the format truly matters, a script can check it (step 10.3), which leaves the people to judge the content.
    3 Sounds authoritativeIt rewards exactly the confident tone that hides invented facts.
    4 Is comprehensiveIt rewards length. In SkillsBench (Li et al., preprint, 2026), comprehensive skills added 0.7 points against 19.0 for compact ones. Those groups may not compare like with like, so treat this as a warning and not a law.
    5 A senior architect is happyWhich one? Anthropic’s test for an eval task is that “two domain experts would independently reach the same pass/fail verdict”. This line fails it.
    6 Everyone agreesIt is a rule about the meeting and not about the output. It also gives every panel member a veto, so nobody answers for the result.

    Set the checks

    Here are seven starting checks, written so that a one-paragraph record and a fourteen-section one can both pass or fail on substance. You will use them in step 13.2.

    • 1 Sourced: every fact traces to a supplied source, or is marked as unverified.
    • 2 Drivers: every driver in the brief appears and is weighed.
    • 3 Reasons: the reason for the choice rests on the drivers, not on words like “modern” or “best practice”.
    • 4 Real cost: it states at least one downside specific to this decision.
    • 5 No filling: it invents no options, owners, numbers or approvals to fill a gap.
    • 6 Gaps raised: every gap or conflict in the sources is raised where a reader will see it, not buried or smoothed over.
    • 7 Expert’s own: your expert’s extra check. If they have none: a reviewer could read this in five minutes.
    1. Name the owner. One person, with real experience of the work, who did not write a competing skill.
    2. Challenge. For each check, the group asks: could two of us read the same output and give different verdicts? What would slip through?
    3. Decide. The owner keeps, rewords or drops each check, and may write the seventh. There is no vote.

    The bake-off page lists these seven checks. If your owner reworded one, keep its number and score against the owner’s wording. Working alone, you are the owner: ask one colleague to attack your two weakest checks, and note that you have skipped the panel.

    Why one owner, and why a panel as well

    These two ideas pull against each other, so we show both. Husain and Shankar argue that “For most small to medium-sized companies, appointing a single domain expert as a ‘benevolent dictator’ is the most effective approach”. They add that larger organisations may need several annotators. This is practitioner judgement from people who teach a paid course, with no comparative data. Aroyo and Welty (2015) list “Disagreement Is Bad”, “One Is Enough” and “Experts Are Better” among their myths of human annotation; that work was on medical relation extraction with crowd workers.

    Our reading: the owner decides what “good” means, because someone must answer for it. Other raters then find what the owner can’t see. Shankar et al. (2024), in a qualitative study of nine practitioners, found that “it is impossible to completely determine evaluation criteria prior to human judging of LLM outputs”. So expect your checks to change after the first round.

    Think deeper: Your owner’s checks will carry their habits as well as their expertise. How would you tell one from the other? What should happen when an owner keeps a check that raters repeatedly can’t apply the same way?

    Who should own what “good” means?

    The pattern

    Decision rights. You know this as the “A” in RACI, a design authority or a product owner: many are consulted and one is accountable. A skill’s checks are a small standard, and the same questions apply as to any standard.

    What is really being decided

    Whose judgement becomes the organisation’s definition of acceptable work once it is built into a shared skill. A skill turns one person’s view into everyone’s default, often without anyone having agreed to that.

    The forces

    • Accountability against breadth: one owner is clear and quick, and has blind spots a panel would catch.
    • Depth against reach: a security lead’s checks should not define a good ADR, and the reverse is just as true, so a skill may need more than one owner.
    • Authority against expertise: the most senior person is not always the one who best knows the work.
    • Time: ownership is unpaid work unless someone funds it, and unfunded owners drift away.

    Left open

    • When a skill crosses two domains, whose check wins?
    • Can someone appeal an owner’s decision, and to whom?
    • Does your organisation count this as part of the owner’s job?
    Turning a judgement into a pass or fail check

    Write each check so that it names something a rater can point at in the output. Then test it: give two people the same output and see whether they reach the same verdict. If they don’t, reword the check or split it. This is the test in Anthropic’s guidance on evals, which is vendor guidance with no study data behind it.

    Have raters work independently first. Husain and Shankar advise: “Have annotators label the same examples independently before they discuss them.” For larger programmes they suggest measuring agreement with Cohen’s Kappa, while noting “Even in larger companies, a single expert is often enough.” If you use a tool, annotation products support this directly. LangSmith’s queues state “Reviewers cannot view the feedback left by other reviewers”, and Braintrust’s blind mode does much the same, with an exception for reviewers holding Update permission. These are product features and not evidence that blind review improves results.

    A correction you may meet elsewhere: Husain did not say raters on a 1 to 5 scale are guessing. His sentence is about whoever prescribes the metrics: “if someone says you need to measure 8 things on a 1-5 scale, they don’t know what they are looking for.”

    Read more

    • Demystifying evals for AI agents (Anthropic)
    • Who Validates the Validators? (Shankar et al., 2024)
    • Truth Is a Lie (Aroyo and Welty, 2015)

  • One named owner, or I as owner, settled the checks for this round.
  • I can explain why the owner decides and why other raters are still needed.

    Run a bake-off

    Three competing ADR skills and no skill at all, on the same brief. Shuffle the outputs, rate them alone, then see who won.

    Step13.2

    Part 13
    Skills as a team
    Time
    20 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    Split into three tables with one brief each, and give each arm to one person so all four chats run at once. Twenty minutes is tight. If you can, generate the outputs before the session and spend the time on rating. Keep authors of any skill away from the shuffling.

    Three skills are competing to write your team’s ADRs. All three, and their listings, are invented for this exercise, so nothing needs downloading. Each one bets on something different.

    SkillIts betIts likely priceIts listing (invented)
    adr-quickA record nobody reads protects nobody. One Y-statement on one screen, and it never asks a question.Little room for drivers and options.3,100 installs. 4.6 stars from 41 ratings.
    adr-gatedThin inputs create false confidence. It stops until the inputs are complete, or until you tell it to go on.An extra turn, every time something is missing.190 installs. No ratings.
    adr-completeThorough records earn trust. Fourteen sections, with gaps filled from industry knowledge.Length, and whatever it fills in.14,200 installs. 4.8 stars from 312 ratings. Featured.

    Run the arms

    1. Take one brief per table. Working alone, take brief 3 first. Our guess, untested, is that it separates the arms most.
    2. Start four fresh chats, outside any project, with the same assistant and model. Turn memory off if you can.
    3. Send the same request in every arm, with the brief pasted below it.
    4. If an arm asks a question, send the standard reply, once. Everything else counts as coaching.
    5. Pass the final output on, unedited. Don’t read the other arms.
    Write this up as a decision record for our architecture review board. That is everything we have. Please go ahead, and mark anything missing.

    Paste the skill in for this exercise. Paste the full skill text at the top of a fresh chat, then the request and the brief. For the no-skill arm, leave the skill out. You can install skills and select one with @, but the pages we could read don’t say how to switch a skill off or how to see that one fired, so a “no skill” run might not be clean. Checked 7 November 2026. Test that in your own workspace if you install them.

    Either way works. Paste the full skill text at the top of a fresh chat, or install the skill and use its toggle in Customize > Skills, because “Disabled skills won’t be available to Claude”. In Cowork and Claude Code, skill-creator “also runs the same prompts without the skill as a baseline”, in parallel. Claude Code also has an optional blind comparison, which needs subagents and so isn’t available in chat. Checked 7 November 2026, so confirm what your surface offers. Run the human rating here regardless.

    Pasting tests what the skill produces and not whether it fires on its own. That is fine here, because a bake-off compares outputs. These briefs are invented. Don’t swap in real work data unless your organisation approves it.

    Shuffle, rate alone, then talk

    In a group, a facilitator who has not seen the runs pastes all four outputs into the panel for that brief and shuffles them on a shared screen. Each rater reads outputs A to D and marks their own sheet in silence. When everyone has finished, go through the sheets row by row. Where people disagree, stop and find out why. Then the owner rules, the facilitator enters the rulings and reveals the labels.

    Working alone, use the panel directly, and get a partner to paste and shuffle if you can. Shuffling your own outputs is less blind, because you have already seen them. Either way, blinding has a limit: a one-paragraph record can only come from one skill. Labels can be hidden and style can’t, which is why the checks ask about content.

  • 4 Real cost: it states at least one downside specific to this decision.
  • 5 No filling: it invents no options, owners, numbers or approvals to fill a gap.
  • 6 Gaps raised: every gap or conflict in the sources is raised where a reader will see it, not buried or smoothed over.

    Read the result

    What each brief was built to test – open after the reveal
    BriefWhat a good record has to deal with
    1 RoutineContent system: 70,000 + 3 × 15,000 = 115,000. Product: 20,000 + 3 × 55,000 = 185,000, which breaks D2. PDF files fail D1 and take 15 working days against D4’s five. The awkward part is that the accessibility rework is not in the cost note [H3], so the chosen option’s real cost is unknown.
    2 ThinThere is one driver, one option, no cost, no vendor and no owner. A sponsor’s “simpler for everyone” is an opinion and not a driver. A good record says all of this, and invents nothing to make the decision look considered.
    3 ConflictThe chosen option breaks ADR-0021 for 410 sensitive datasets, and no exception is recorded [R1, R2]. Two sources price it differently: 95,000 [R3] and 70,000 [R4]. The onshore region misses D2 by nine months. The own platform costs 210,000 in its first year, which breaks D3, and misses D2 as well. No option meets all three drivers. The sponsor’s “read as settled” is no reason to hide any of it.

    We haven’t published a “right” winner, because we haven’t piloted this set. Your result is the result, for your assistant, model and raters.

    Keep the no-skill arm in every comparison, because published results vary so widely. SkillsBench (Li et al., preprint, 2026) found curated skills raised average pass rates from 33.9% to 50.5% over 87 tasks. SWE-Skills-Bench (Han et al., preprint, 2026) found average pass ratios of 76.59% without skills and 76.93% with them, and 92 of 98 skills showed no statistically significant effect. Its authors stress that this means “no directional effect was detected with ten requirements, not that the effect is zero”. It also found 40 of 98 skills changed sign between two harnesses running the same model. The two studies differ in design, so don’t average them. Our reading: a winner on your assistant is a winner on your assistant. And one run per arm on one brief is a rough check, not a measurement.

    Extension: add a real community skill. Swap your weakest arm for a real ADR skill from a public registry. Don’t paste it anywhere until you have read every file and worked through Anthropic’s eight-step review checklist, as in steps 2.2 and 10.2. Check its licence too. Liu et al. (preprint, 2026) detected at least one vulnerability in 26.1% of 31,132 skills. Those are detected patterns and not attacks seen working, but they are why the review comes first.

    Think deeper: Your winner beat the incumbent by one check on one brief. The incumbent’s author is in the room, and forty people already use it. What result would you require before replacing a skill people rely on? Who may call for a rerun, and how would you stop people rerunning until their favourite wins?

    How much comparison does a skill deserve?

    The pattern

    Vendor selection with a proof of concept: you agree the scoring before the demonstrations, so the slickest demo can’t rewrite the criteria. The no-skill arm is the option every good procurement carries, which is to do nothing.

    What is really being decided

    Whether the organisation wants one standard skill or a small set routed by situation, and how much evidence it takes to change a standard. A bake-off has a cost of its own, and that needs to be weighed against what a wrong choice would cost.

    The forces

    • One standard against local fit: one skill is easier to own and improve, and may suit no team very well.
    • Evidence against speed: a rigorous comparison can take longer than the difference is worth.
    • Result against shelf life: a vendor’s model update can change the ranking with no change on your side.
    • Fairness against pride: people’s work loses in public, and they may stop contributing if that is handled badly.

    Left open

    • What margin of victory justifies the cost of switching?
    • Who pays for raters’ time, and from which budget?
    • Should a team be allowed to opt out of the winner, and on what evidence?
    Making a comparison hold up

    Repeat runs

    Models vary between runs, so one output per arm can’t separate a small difference from noise. The Agent Skills evaluation guide says standard deviation “is only meaningful with multiple runs per eval”, and it sets no fixed number. claude plugin eval runs each case “three times by default” per arm, with and without the plugin. You would compare competitors by running each one against the same no-plugin baseline. Its case files and skill-creator’s are not interchangeable.

    Selective reruns

    The Leaderboard Illusion (Singh et al., preprint, 2025) reports that providers tested private variants and disclosed selectively, giving biased scores on a public leaderboard. The Arena’s reply disputes several claims, and the lead authors work at a ranked provider. Applying it to teams is our inference: run every arm the same number of times, and report them all.

    Using a model as the judge

    The Agent Skills guide offers an LLM judge as an optional blind comparison. Treat it as a second reader and not as the owner. Zheng et al. (NeurIPS 2023) showed position bias and verbosity bias. Our reading: verbosity bias could favour the long skill in this bake-off. They found GPT-4 and humans agreed 85% of the time on non-tie votes, and 66% with ties counted. Shuffle the order if you use one.

    The formats in this bake-off

    adr-quick uses Zimmermann’s six-part Y-statement. adr-gated uses MADR 4.0, which is dual-licensed under MIT and CC0. adr-complete is a composite of habits we invented; it isn’t based on any real skill.

    Read more

    • Evaluating skills (Agent Skills)
    • Architecture decision making, with Y-statements (Zimmermann)
    • Evaluating Skills, Not Just Agents (Kevin et al., 2026)
    • Detecting and Understanding Malicious Agent Skills in the Wild (Liu et al., 2026) – for the extension: 157 confirmed of 98,380, which the authors call a lower bound
  • I wrote down my prediction before running anything.
  • I scored at least one brief across all four arms before seeing the labels.
  • I looked at where raters split, or at where I hesitated, and what that says about the checks.
  • I can say whether no skill beat any of the three.

    Own it

    A winning skill with no owner decays quietly. Fill in a register entry and a submission card, and check who can publish in your workspace.

    Step13.3

    Part 13
    Skills as a team
    Time
    15 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    The register entry is the deliverable. If you are short of time, fill in the card’s first and sixth fields only. If an admin is in the room, ask them to read out the real publishing setting, because it often surprises people.

    Your winner is shared on a Friday. Six months later it has been copied into nine repositories and the model underneath has changed twice.

    Gao et al. (preprint, 2026) studied reuse in public repositories and concluded that “reuse is largely a one-time copy operation: most reused skills remain near-verbatim, 53% are never modified after adoption, and subsequent local maintenance is overwhelmingly additive”. Read the 53% carefully. It covers 2,462 reused software engineering skills from one registry and public repositories only, in a one-year window to May 2026, on a format launched in October 2025. The copies are young, so later changes may still come. The study also didn’t test whether an unmodified copy does any harm. In a separate dataset, GitSkills (Destefanis et al., to appear at MSR ’27) found 50.5% of 3.8 million SKILL.md files were byte-for-byte copies of another file.

    Our reading: copying is not the failure. The failure is that nobody is responsible for the copy.

    Fill in the register

    Write an entry for your bake-off’s winner. If no skill won, write one for the skill you would keep anyway, and put that result in the eval line. Use a real name for the owner. If you can’t name one, that is your finding: the skill shouldn’t be published yet.

    “Tier” comes from step 12.1. The fields build on the registry Anthropic recommends: purpose, owner, version, dependencies and evaluation status. We added a deputy, a next review date and a way out, because those are what fail when an owner moves on.

    Fill in the submission card

    The card is what a new skill arrives with. Its first seven fields follow the UK Government’s AI Knowledge Hub template for shared prompts: what it does; what to do before use; how people customise it; how it works; what to do after use; level of verification; and the prompt itself. On 7 November 2026 the Hub listed 47 prompts, 17 of them marked Verified, which it defines as “reviewed and approved by professionals in their subject”.

    That badge is a good idea with a gap. The Hub publishes no process behind “Verified”, no evidence that verified prompts perform better, and “level of verification” is the submitter’s own statement. So our card changes that field: the level names a person and a date, and “Verified” can only come from the owner, for a stated use. We also added an evidence section.

    Find out who can already publish

    Your register means little if anyone can publish around it. Go and look at the real setting, or ask whoever can. What follows was checked on 7 November 2026. Vendor features change, so confirm it in your own workspace.

    Check: workspace settings, under Permissions & roles. OpenAI says owners control who can create, share and install skills through Permissions and Roles or RBAC, and that sharing depends on workspace settings. A help article appears to list separate toggles for enabling, uploading, sharing, publishing to the workspace and installing for others. We could only see that in a search result, so check it for yourself. We could not settle the current default, so don’t assume one.

    Note: skills can reach people by three separate paths: workspace Skills, local files and plugins. OpenAI says “Moving a skill doesn’t transfer ChatGPT workspace ownership, sharing, role assignments”, so a register entry needs to say which path it covers.

    Check: Organization settings > Plugins & skills > Policy. The options are Requires review, Open and Off. Don’t assume yours is “Open” or “Requires review”: the default depends on your plan and your history, as the figure below shows.

    Note: Open means published without review. A reviewer, when there is one, sees what changed since the published version, up to three possible duplicates and the scan result. Scanning is Enterprise only, and doesn’t cover “Skills you create with Claude”. A pass “isn’t a guarantee that a skill is safe in every respect”. The article also says “Your own submissions don’t go through review”, so test who that covers in your organisation. It may leave your separation of duties to you.

    Two more lines from that article are worth knowing. “If the author leaves, the published item stays in the library”, so a skill can outlive everyone who understands it. And “When you approve a new version, everyone who uses the item gets the update automatically”, so approval is effectively a release to production.

    Think deeper: In a team of four, the best author is also the natural owner, and “authors don’t review their own skills” can’t be staffed easily. What is the smallest separation of duties you would still trust? Which role could you safely combine, and which never?

    Who may publish, and through what gate?

    The pattern

    Inner source, with trusted committers and CODEOWNERS, plus the segregation of duties you already apply to code and finance. It behaves like a CI gate on a shared library: anyone may propose, a named few may merge, and every change is tested.

    What is really being decided

    Where the control point sits, in your repository or in the platform’s library setting, and which one wins when they disagree. A team can have a strict pull request process while the workspace setting lets anyone publish around it.

    The forces

    • Open against gated: open publishing gets more contributions and more duplicates, while review gets quality and queues.
    • Security review against domain review: a scan or a security reader can’t tell you whether an ADR skill’s advice is sound, and an architect may miss a data leak.
    • Automatic updates against pinning: everyone gets the fix at once, and everyone gets the regression too.
    • Reviewer time: a gate nobody funds becomes a queue people learn to avoid.

    Left open

    • Is your repository or your platform’s library the source of truth, and what stops them drifting apart?
    • What must happen when an owner leaves and no deputy is named?
    • Do low-tier skills need the whole gate, or a lighter one?
    One repository: what goes in it, and how it reaches people

    Source control

    Anthropic’s enterprise guidance says to store skill directories in Git and keep them as “the single source of truth”, because “Custom Skills do not sync across surfaces”. It also advises pinning skills to specific versions in production, keeping the previous version as a fallback, computing checksums of reviewed skills and using signed commits.

    Getting it to people

    • Claude: on Team and Enterprise, organisation sync reads a marketplace repository through a GitHub or GitLab connection, and on github.com and gitlab.com that repository must be private or internal. Claude Code can pin an entry to a ref or sha. See Host and maintain a marketplace. Checked 7 November 2026.
    • ChatGPT: “You need to be a workspace admin” to import a GitHub marketplace, public or private, and new marketplaces sync each day. The supported files include a “Claude-compatible marketplace” at .claude-plugin/marketplace.json, so one repository may be able to serve both. Test that before relying on it. See OpenAI’s plugin management page. It is read through a summarising fetch, so confirm the wording. Checked 7 November 2026.

    What Thoughtworks says

    This is consultancy judgement and not measurement. The Radar’s current entry is Agent plugin marketplace: Trial, 4 November 2026. Two earlier entries are not on the current edition (Vol 35), though the Radar says a blip from the last few editions is likely still relevant. Curated shared instructions for software teams was Adopt in November 2025 and April 2026, and it says that “relying on individual developers to write prompts from scratch is emerging as an anti-pattern”. Claude Code plugin marketplace was Trial in April 2026, noting that copying instructions from external sources “often led to version drift”.

    Spread and retire

    Help the skill spread through peers, decide when it should stop, then close the series with a plan you can start on Monday.

    Step13.4

    Part 13
    Skills as a team
    Time
    20 min
    Last reviewed
    7 November 2026

    Keep the last five minutes for plans and don’t let the retirement discussion eat them. Pair people up and have each read their plan aloud to the other. End there, not with a summary from the front.

    A shared skill can win a bake-off, have an owner and still fail in two opposite ways. Nobody may use it, or everyone may go on using it long after it has stopped helping.

    Spreading it

    Plan on spreading skills through peers more than through a central library, and hold that view loosely. The evidence is indirect. DORA’s 2019 report found low performers favour training centres and centres of excellence, “strategies that create more silos and isolated expertise”, while communities of practice were more common among higher performers. That is observational, about DevOps and from before generative AI, and elite performers still reported centres of excellence at 24%.

    Time matters too. DORA’s report on generative AI (2025) says that dedicated time during work hours to explore AI tools “leads to a 131% increase in team AI adoption”. That is the report’s wording for a statistical estimate from survey data, so read it as “associated with”. It measures developers’ adoption and not learning or quality. In the same report, clear acceptable-use policies came out at +451%.

    Three moves follow, by our reading: have a respected peer show the skill on real work, put an hour in the diary, and collect examples from your own domain.

    What nobody has shown yet. We found no study showing that shared skills improve a team’s results. Adoption is not proof, and neither is a bake-off. Keep your own before-and-after numbers, because at the moment they may be the best evidence you can get.

    Keep, fix or retire?

    Here are four invented skills from one register. Place each one, and decide what you would do, before you open the answer.

    What we would do – open after placing all four
    SkillCornerWhy
    Meeting minutes summary3The busiest skill here, and it adds nothing since the upgrade. Fix it, or tell people they can stop using it.
    Capability map checker2Rarely used and valuable, so a usage rule alone would have retired it. Keep it.
    ADR writer for last year’s template1Set a date and remove it. Those two monthly runs are producing the wrong format.
    This year’s ADR skill4Keep it, and rerun the eval on the review date and after any model change.

    You will have to design retirement yourself. Anthropic’s guidance says to “Deprecate Skills when evaluations consistently fail or the workflow is retired”, but its own marketplace documentation states “there is no deprecation state”. We found no such state documented for ChatGPT either, in the pages we could read.

    What we found: if you remove a plugin from an imported marketplace, its workspace copy stays and is marked “No longer in source”. So removing it from Git doesn’t remove it from people’s view. Help articles we could see only in search results suggest that Enterprise and Edu workspace analytics show skill usage, so ask your admin what they can see, and test how a removal behaves before you rely on it. Checked 7 November 2026.

    What we found: owners can use “Remove from library” for a provisioned skill. In a Claude Code marketplace you remove the entry and map its name to null in renames. Without forceRemoveDeletedPlugins, a removed plugin stays installed. /skill-doctor shows what each skill costs and how often it is used, and flags skills never invoked. It needs v2.1.252 or later, and it excludes bundled and enterprise skills. Checked 7 November 2026. Test this in your own setup.

    Think deeper: A skill now ties with no skill, but a senior leader’s team loves it and says it saves them time. The eval says one thing and the users say another. What would you need to know to tell whether your checks are missing something real, or the team just likes the habit? Who decides, and would they say so in public?

    You have finished Part 13, and the series

    PartYou can now
    5 · Step 5.1Test whether a skill fires when it should, and whether it beats no skill at all.
    6 · Step 6.1Build a skill that drafts from a template, with gotchas taken from reviewers’ comments.
    7 · Step 7.1Check output separately from the skill that wrote it, and test the checker itself.
    8 · Step 8.1Set hard limits on what a skill may decide, and test them under pressure.
    9 · Step 9.1Tie advice to a pinned source, and have it say “not stated”.
    10 · Step 10.1Separate what a script should do from what needs judgement, and read code before you run it.
    11 · Step 11.1Connect a skill to live data with its permissions and injection risks in view.
    12 · Step 12.1Chain skills into a controlled process, scaled to the consequence, and show whether it earns its cost.
    13 · Step 13.1Choose between skills on evidence, name who owns what “good” means, and plan how a skill stops.

    In all nine, a named person keeps the decision. That has been the thread throughout: models draft and check, and people answer for the result.

    A last honest note. Most of the research on skills is preprint and less than two years old, and nobody has yet measured whether teaching this method changes what teams produce. Treat it as a good starting method, and keep your own numbers.

    How to start on Monday

    Don’t start with a platform or a library. Start with one correction you are tired of making.

    1. Monday, 30 minutes. Pick one piece of work you repeat, where reviewers keep raising the same fault. Write three pass or fail checks for it. Run the task with no skill and score the result. That is your baseline (step 5.3).
    2. This week. Write the smallest skill that fixes that fault, using the corrections as its gotchas (step 6.3). Run it against the baseline on three tasks. If it doesn’t win, delete it. That counts as a useful result.
    3. This month. If it wins, add one independent check (step 7.3), and ask a colleague to break it.
    4. When a second person wants it. That is when you name an owner, put it in a repository and write a register row. Run a bake-off only when real alternatives exist.

    Write your plan as an if-then, tied to a real moment in your week. Gollwitzer and Sheeran’s meta-analysis (2006) pooled 94 tests at d = .65, and a 2024 update of 642 tests puts the range at .27 to .66 by outcome. We read only the abstracts, and neither studied architects, so applying them here is our inference. It costs one sentence to try.

    Export your notes for yourself or share them with your facilitator. The notes stay on your device unless you decide to share them.

    Community of practice or centre of excellence?

    The pattern

    The internal developer platform and inner source. A small platform team provides the paved road: the repository, the eval harness, the register and the publishing gate. Domain experts own the content. You have seen this argument before over shared services, and over architecture functions themselves.

    What is really being decided

    Not one or the other but which jobs sit where. Those jobs are: who may publish, who owns “good” in each domain, how people’s time is funded, and what happens to a skill when its owner leaves. The risk at one extreme is a central library nobody uses. At the other, it is fifty unowned copies that nobody can find or fix.

    The forces

    • Consistency against relevance: a centre standardises, and peers know what the work really needs.
    • Funded against voluntary: communities run on goodwill that disappears in a busy quarter, while centres have budgets and need to justify them.
    • Speed against assurance: a community spreads a useful skill quickly, and it can spread a faulty one just as quickly.
    • Evidence: the DORA comparison is indirect, and nothing we read tests either model for skills.

    Left open

    • Which of those four jobs would you keep central, and which would you hand to domains?
    • Whose budget pays for an owner’s time, and for how long?
    • At what number of skills or teams would your answer change?
    Retiring a skill with no platform support

    When to act

    Anthropic’s enterprise guidance ties actions to eval signals. Declining trigger accuracy means updating the description or instructions. Coexistence conflicts mean consolidating or narrowing. Consistently low quality means rewriting. “Persistent failures across updates” means deprecating. It also advises rerunning evals “periodically to detect drift or regressions as workflows and models evolve”. A vendor model update counts as a change, even when nothing changed on your side.

    Merging instead of retiring

    Where two skills overlap, the same guidance says to merge them “only when the consolidated Skill’s evaluations confirm equivalent performance to the individual Skills it replaces”. Run the retiring skills’ test cases against the merged one.

    What each platform does

    • Claude organisation library: “Remove from library” for a provisioned skill. Turning Publishing off doesn’t remove what is already published: “Published items stay in the library until an owner removes them.”
    • Claude Code marketplace: “there is no deprecation state”. The documented route is to remove the entry, map its name to null in renames, and optionally set forceRemoveDeletedPlugins. Users then see “Removed from the … marketplace”.
    • ChatGPT: a removed marketplace plugin’s workspace copy is marked “No longer in source”. A help article snippet says “Delete skill permanently removes the skill from the workspace”. We couldn’t open that article, so check it in your own workspace.
